## Fix: a live turn runs one task before its slice can end it (criterion 5, 2026-11-15)

Task: the 16 MiB sheet ramp `sheety_16383` did not finish since PR #541 (class atoms; "Final benchmark of the perf goal, round 2"). Machine archMachine. Raw logs and scripts are machine-local under `/data/claude-tmp/j/` and `/data/claude-tmp/`. Main at the start: `16b39b5a` (it has #551, #554, #555).

### Cause (verified)

- Reproduced on `16b39b5a`: the page does not finish in 20 s. With counters in `feed_styles` it ran more than 1,000 passes with `tasks 0`; `style_availability` said `Ready` each time. Every pass came from `Page::tick` → `settle` → `Session::resume` → `Run::resume`, so the loop was in the ticks of the page, not in one call.
- A live turn has a slice of 8 ms (`SLICE`, set when the turn starts). `Run::resume` calls `feed_styles` first, then goes on with the scripts or the rounds. In a split document `sliced()` is checked before each script and at the top of each round. One `feed_styles` of the 16 MiB sheet takes 1.2 to 5 ms for the first passes and 9 ms (`plan` 8.7 to 9.0 ms) from the sixth on; `plan` copies the sheet text once (`add`: `text.to_string()`), and `style_availability` throws the copy away. Timed with `Instant` around `feed_styles` and `plan`, 12 first calls and each 500th (`DBG` build, not kept).
- So each turn spent its whole slice on the style pass, `sliced()` was true before the first script (or the first round), and the turn ended with `Settled` and no work done. The next turn did the same. The page never ran its second script or its `load` event. The cost of a turn did not change with the number of turns, so this is a livelock, not a slow loop.
- Why a sheet of half the size works: the pass is 4.5 ms, below the slice. Why it worked at `4a27b7a9`: hypothesis (not measured): the pass cost then was below 8 ms. I did not time `feed_styles` on `4a27b7a9`. #541 changed allocation, and the copy of a 16 MiB block (page faults of a fresh mapping) varies from 1.2 to 9 ms between passes in the same process.
- The earlier hypothesis of round 2 ("`add` copies the text again and again; each call is a few ms") was right about the symbol and wrong about the shape: it is not a call count that grows with the rules (about 100,000 calls); it is a loop of ticks that never ends because no tick makes progress.
- It also explains why the driver `--timeout` did not stop it. See "Driver" below.

### Change

- `Run::sliced` is true only after the turn has run one task or one round (`res.tasks + res.rounds > 0`). A turn that is late before it starts still does one unit of work, so the page moves on. No limit, no budget and no time-out was added; the slice is the same 8 ms for a turn that has done something.
- `PageLimits::slice` (default `SLICE`) so a test can set the slice. The two places that made the slice read it.

Complexity. B is the sheet bytes, S the slice, T the tasks of the page. Before: a turn costs Θ(B) before its first task; with Θ(B) ≥ S no turn runs a task, so the work is unbounded (no end). After: each turn runs at least one task, so the page ends in at most T + rounds turns; each turn still pays one Θ(B) pass (not changed, see below), so the total is O(T·B) in the worst case and 8 to 9 turns for this page.

### Test

`browser_session_tests::a_live_turn_with_its_slice_used_up_still_runs_one_script`: a live session with a sheet and two scripts, `slice` zero (every turn starts late). It fails before the change ("the page did not load in 5 s") and passes after (0.01 s).

### Numbers (run counts: 3, interleaved, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, peak RSS by `wait4`; spread under 0.01% on instructions)

| Page | `4a27b7a9` | main `16b39b5a` | NEW |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `sheety_16383` instructions (M) | 5,404.1 (5,404.08 to 5,404.10) | no result in 40 to 90 s (4 tries) | 5,320.4 (5,320.37 to 5,320.42) |
| `sheety_16383` peak RSS (MiB) | 274.1 | - | 216.5 (216.4 to 216.7) |
| `sheety_8192` instructions (M) | 2,717.4 | - | 2,679.6 |
| `sheety_8192` peak RSS (MiB) | 144.9 | - | 115.8 |

Criterion 5 (300 MiB or lower): **met, 216.5 MiB**.

- Ramps, main `16b39b5a` against NEW, 3 runs each: `rest_2` to `rest_1000` (12 pages) and `compm_1000` to `compm_34000` (15 pages): the instructions differ by at most 0.003% (spread), peak RSS by at most 1.1% (noise, 0.5 MiB at most). Example: `rest_13` 1,042.52 M and 1,042.53 M, `compm_22000` 391.26 M and 391.26 M, `rest_1000` 47,084.1 M and 47,084.9 M. The ramps do not run split live turns, so they do not move.
- `bare-stress scale css`, 2 runs each, main against NEW: 148 case rows, the 76 of 5 MB or more: 0 differ by more than 2% in peak MB; no status differs.
- 47 journeys (`tools/bench/journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`, corpus `virtual-load`, `nextjs-docs` skipped): 47 pass on both, no replay miss, sum of medians 73,185.2 M against 73,185.1 M (-0.0%, no journey over +0.1%). PSS sum -8.9% and RSS sum +0.1%: the PSS sample is noise (a sample every 20 ms; no journey changed in instructions).
- Cost matrix against main (805 rows, 803 measured, glibc and jemalloc, base dir built with `--workspace --examples -p bare-stress`, then `-p bare-drive -p bare-stress`): **0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators**, 0 under one. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` fail to run on both (the known stack overflow).
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 4,061 passed, 9 failed. 7 are the known openssl TLS tests. `external_sheets_embedded_sheets_and_inline_styles_cascade_in_order` and `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` are the known flaky ones: both pass when run alone.
- test262: exit 0, gate ok, 29,731 pass (checkout at `e4fbf577`). `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh` (page `typing-page-lazy-arrow`): 278.3 M for each key (`#a1`), 283.6 M (`#f0`), load and mount 591.1 M, RSS 30.7 MiB at 50 keys, equal on main and NEW. No file of `crates/js` changed; these three are for the record.

### Driver

The driver `--timeout` does not stop this page for another reason, in `Page::wait_load`: the loop `continue`s when a tick ran, and it checks the time limit only after a tick that did nothing. A page that always has work (here the split document that "goes on at once") never reaches the check. The steps of the ramp finish; then `Session::finish` calls `wait_load(END_LOAD_WAIT)` (5 s) and spins in it with no end. Verified: with `--timeout 3000` the old binary ran 90 s; the debug build showed the steps passing and more than 600 ticks inside the last call. This is fixed in a second PR (see the section "Fix: `wait_load` checks its time limit after a tick that ran").

### Not tested

Wall time on an idle machine. Windows and macOS. The pass cost on `4a27b7a9` (so "why #541" is a hypothesis). A page with many scripts and a large sheet (each turn still pays one Θ(B) pass; see below).

### Noticed, not changed

- Each turn of `Run::resume` calls `feed_styles` without the `still()` check that `feed_if_ran` uses, and `style_availability` makes a copy of every sheet text in `plan` that it throws away. A page with a 16 MiB sheet pays about 9 ms for each turn for this. A guard on `still()` is not safe as it is: a preload that finished with no change of the tree is not in the stamp. Not touched.

## Fix: `wait_load` checks its time limit after a tick that ran (2026-11-15)

Second part of the task of "Fix: a live turn runs one task before its slice can end it" (PR #562): the driver `--timeout` did not stop the page of `sheety_16383`.

### Cause (verified)

`Page::wait_load(limit)` ran `tick` in a loop and `continue`d when the tick ran. It checked `limit` only after a tick that did nothing. A page that always has work never reaches that check: here a split document that waits for a script has a timer that is due, so `work()` is true and each tick "ran". `Session::finish` calls `wait_load(END_LOAD_WAIT)` (5 s) after the last step, so a driver run whose steps all passed spun in it with no end, whatever `--timeout` said. Seen on the binary of `294f1c01` (the page livelock of PR #562) with `--timeout 3000` and steps of `open` and two `expect js`: 90 s with no result; the page thread used the CPU and the main thread waited on the join; a debug build showed the three steps pass and more than 600 ticks inside the one last call.

### Change

In `wait_load`, a tick that ran also checks the limit (`vclock::instant() >= end`) and returns the same error as the idle case ("the time limit passed before load"). Before: the loop ended at the limit only after an idle tick (O(ticks until idle), unbounded). After: it ends at the first tick after the limit.

### Test

`crates/drive/tests/wait_load_limit.rs`: a page with a due timer and a script that the server holds for 3 s; `wait_load(300 ms)` must return an error in under 1.5 s. Before: it took 3.0 s and the page loaded (the test failed). After: 0.30 s.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 4,062 passed, 9 failed: the 7 known openssl TLS tests, `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` and `a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero` (known flaky under load).
- Cost matrix against main `241fa13d` (805 rows, 803 measured, both allocators): 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators; `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` fail to run (known).

### Not tested

The end-to-end case (driver `--timeout` on the livelocked page) after the fix: PR #562 removed the livelock, so no page that I have hangs any more; the test stands for it. The 47 journeys and the ramps (the added check runs once for each tick that ran; no instruction row moved in the matrix). Windows and macOS.

## Gmail load: why bare is slower than Chrome (research, 2026-11-15)

Task R2-G. Docs only. Design: [design-gmail-load.md](design-gmail-load.md). Main `b5efbde0`, archMachine (load 2.2 to 4.4 at the start of the bare runs). A temporary probe (a mark at the first `tr.zA` row, and a timer per script) was used and is not in the repository. Safety: read-only runs, bare's saved session, Chrome's `chrome-auto` profile with one new tab per run. No account detail is in the document. The raw recordings (network records, perf data, Chrome traces) are only under `/data/bare-tmp/gmail-profile/` and `/data/bare-tmp/r2/gmail-load/raw/` because they hold session data.

Results.
- The "8x" of #548 compares bare's `open` return (21.1 to 22.4 s) with Chrome's first row (1.2 s). At the same event, the first row, bare needs 4.28 to 4.52 s (3 runs) and Chrome 1.16 to 1.47 s (9 runs, cache on, cache off, and cold with the service worker bypassed; one cold run 2.20 s). That is about 3.4x. The 9 s of #548 came from `eval` running the page for about 8 s.
- Instructions at the first row: bare 17.1 G (samples; 18.0 to 20.5 G by 0.5 s intervals), Chrome 12 to 19.6 G (whole cgroup). Whole start-up: bare 104.5 to 108.3 G, Chrome 52 to 57 G after 30 s. bare reaches Chrome's 47 G (6 s) at about 8 s.
- bare is idle until the document ends (2.0 s). Its first byte is at 1.24 s; cold Chrome's is at 0.43 s, and Chrome starts the scripts then. bare starts them at 2.03 s. After the document bare needs 2.5 s and 17 G to the first row; Chrome's main thread is busy 1.42 s (JS self 0.80 s, compile 0.33 s).
- Same code: at the first row bare has 3.02 M calls and Chrome 4.06 M (0.74); the top functions are within 0.72x to 0.96x. Without `navigator.serviceWorker` bare gets a 325 KB document, Chrome cold 447 KB.
- Subsystems, whole run (107.4 G): JS interpreter 78.9%, bindings 4.6%, JS parse 4.5% (13.5% to the first row), allocator 4.0%, style 3.0%, GC 1.6%, layout 1.2%. Network, TLS and decompression are 0.7% after the document. The interpreter costs 389 instructions per step and 5.7 K per call (44.0 M steps, 3.02 M calls to the first row). 83% of the steps are in `m=b`, 14% in `m=ebdd,…`. Top-level scripts run in 0.6 s in total.
- Settle: not a rule problem. The start-up work ends at about 19 s in bare and at 14 to 22 s in Chrome (96% of Chrome's calls by 13.6 s).

Recommendation (ranked): B1 make the document request equal to Chrome's (first byte 1.24 s against 0.43 s; hypothesis), A1 stream the document and start its scripts at the first bytes (first row 4.4 s to about 2.5 to 3 s; hypothesis), C1 slim the call path (-4% instructions), C2 and C3 parse and code cache, C4 bytecode (stopped by the owner).

Not tested: Chrome's renderer instructions alone; bare's call count at the end of `open`; the effect of Chrome's headers or a service-worker stub on bare; a quiet machine (wall times are an upper bound); mail open, search, compose.

## Gmail PR 1 (design 1): the document request equals Chrome's, and why the first byte is late (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): build design 1 of [design-gmail-load.md](design-gmail-load.md) (make the document request equal to Chrome's), then design 2 (stream the document into the parser). Main `93c8b27e`, archMachine. This section is design 1. Safety as in #565: read only, bare's saved session, Chrome only through CDP on `chrome-auto` with one new tab per run (closed after), no cookie copied, no account detail written. Raw data (timings only, no mail) is under `/data/bare-tmp/gmail-stream/`.

Built. A document request (`load_document`: the address bar, `location.assign`, a link, a form, a redirect hop) now sends what Chrome 155 sends on a navigation: `Upgrade-Insecure-Requests: 1`, `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document`, `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate`, `Sec-Fetch-Site` and, for a load that the user started, `Sec-Fetch-User: ?1`. `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `none` (no page started the load), `same-origin`, `same-site` or `cross-site` (the page that started it, by `metadata_site` of PR #479), and a redirect keeps the least trusted value. The Fetch Metadata headers go only to a potentially trustworthy target; `Upgrade-Insecure-Requests` goes to every target. `Next.from` now holds the URL of the initiating page, not its site, because the origin is needed for `same-origin`; `load_document` takes the site for the cookie rules from it. Two tests, written first (they failed on empty headers): `a_load_that_no_page_started_sends_the_navigation_metadata`, `a_navigation_by_the_page_is_same_origin_and_has_no_user_flag_and_a_redirect_keeps_the_least_trusted_site`.

Measured: what Chrome sends (CDP `requestWillBeSentExtraInfo`, 5 cold runs, cache off, service worker bypassed). The document is `GET /mail/u/0/` over HTTP/2, `accept-encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd`, the response is `content-encoding: gzip` and `vary: Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Site`. bare did not send `sec-fetch-*`, `upgrade-insecure-requests`, `priority`, `dnt`, the high-entropy `sec-ch-ua-*` hints, `x-client-data` (a Chrome variations header) and the `x-browser-*` headers. Chrome's cookie header has 24 names, bare's saved session sends 17 (missing: `AEC`, `GMAIL_LF`, `SEARCH_SAMESITE`, `__Host-GMAIL_SCH`, `__Secure-1PSIDTS`, `__Secure-3PSIDTS`). The state file is from 2026-11-13.

Result: none of these changes the first byte. The time from request to the response head ("ttfb" of `bare_net::trace`) of the document is bimodal in bare: about 1.0 to 1.18 s (slow) or about 0.41 to 0.52 s (fast). Chrome (cold, same account, 5 runs of this task and 18 requests of #565): 0.38 to 0.53 s every time. Experiments, each with the probe build of `93c8b27e` (one run each unless a count is given; "slow" is 1.0 to 1.15 s):

| Change on the document request | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline, no change: the first document of a new process (48 runs, in 9 groups over 2 hours) | 39 slow, 9 fast (0.43 to 0.58 s) |
| `Sec-Fetch-*` and `Upgrade-Insecure-Requests` (the built change, 6 runs alternating with the baseline) | 5 slow, 1 fast. Baseline in the same alternation: 6 slow |
| Full Chrome header set (client hints, `Accept-Language: en-IN,...`, `Priority`, `DNT`, `Sec-Fetch-*`) | slow |
| `Accept-Encoding`: `gzip`, `gzip, deflate, br, zstd`, `identity` | all slow. The wire size is 333 KB with gzip and br, 2.3 MB with identity |
| Connect to Chrome's address (142.251.106.19) or to bare's (142.250.77.101), 3 runs each | all slow |
| A copy of the session file, saved after one load (37 cookies, with `SEARCH_SAMESITE`, a second `COMPASS`), 6 runs | 5 slow, 1 fast. The original: 6 slow |
| A gap of 1, 10 or 20 s after another bare run | slow |
| A first load of 15 s, then a new process at once (3 pairs) | the second process: 2 slow, 1 fast |
| The same process, later documents (`location.assign`, the first load ran 8 s, 4 processes) | 10 of 10 fast (0.39 to 0.46 s) |
| The same process, later documents, loads of 3 s each, a new connection each (`fresh`, 4 processes, documents 2 to 4) | 8 of 12 fast; the 4 slow ones are the second or third |

The headers were checked on the wire against a local echo server (the override reached the request). The same TLS stack and network are not slow for other requests: `logstreamz` waits 330 to 343 ms in bare and 341 ms (median, n = 6) in Chrome; `cleardot.gif` 22 to 25 ms in both. So the extra time is only on the document, and it is the server's wait before the first byte, not a client cost. A fast document makes the first row 0.6 s earlier (3.44 to 3.67 s against 4.04 to 4.83 s).

Reading. The headers, the encoding, the address, the cookie set of the file, the connection and the gap between runs are not the cause. Hypothesis: the wait is the server's state for this account or session, not a property of the request. The first document of a new process is slow in 39 of 48 runs; later documents of a process that has been running for 8 s or more are fast in 10 of 10. The state is not in the saved cookies (the copy saved after a load is not faster), not the connection (a new connection is fast too), and not the page activity of an earlier process (a 15 s run does not make the next process fast). Chrome keeps Gmail tabs and service workers alive, so its state may always be warm (to verify). Candidates left, not tested: a session cookie that `save_state` does not write, the TLS ClientHello of the hand-written stack (it is not Chrome's; `logstreamz` through the same stack is as fast as in Chrome, so this is the weaker one), `Cookie` header order and size. To verify: a run of the same `curl` or Chrome request with a cookie set that is cut in steps (Chrome through CDP `Fetch.requestPaused`, which does not change the profile).

Numbers (probe build; the probe is the one of #565: `/data/bare-tmp/r2/gmail-load/probe.patch`, not in the repository). Alternating base and branch, 6 runs each, machine load average 11.7 to 3.5 during the 12 runs (the base always ran first in a pair, so its first rows are the more loaded ones):

| | base `93c8b27e` | branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First byte of the document | 1.16, 1.17, 1.19, 1.21, 1.22, 1.22 s | 0.59 (a fast run), 1.16, 1.17, 1.17, 1.20, 1.23 s |
| First row (`tr.zA`) | 4.20, 4.49, 4.51, 4.55, 4.70, 4.83 s | 3.67, 4.25, 4.33, 4.42, 4.45, 4.45 s |
| Instructions to the first row | 16.5 to 16.8 G | 16.6 to 16.8 G |
| Peak RSS (`VmHWM`, 5.5 s window) | 240 to 250 MiB | 242 to 255 MiB (277 in the fast run) |

Instructions do not change. The time difference of the first row is the load and the one fast run: without it, the branch is 4.25 to 4.45 s. No gain in the first byte is claimed.

Checks (branch `f39d5163` on main `93c8b27e`, archMachine, load 4 to 6):
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 4,065 passed, 8 failed, 15 ignored. The 8 are on main too and are not from this change: the 7 openssl TLS tests and `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` (flaky under load). A first run also had `external_sheets_embedded_sheets_and_inline_styles_cascade_in_order` fail once (known flaky); it passed in the second run.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against main `93c8b27e` (803 rows): 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators; mean change glibc -0.005%, jemalloc +0.000%; 2 rows fail to run (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`: stack overflow, on main too).
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss` (corpus `virtual-load`): 0 replay misses, all pass; sum of median instructions 73,186.7 M base and 73,178.2 M new (-0.0%), largest spread 0.3%; the sum of PSS medians moved -5.8% (noise: single journeys move +7.8% and -2.4% with no instruction change).
- `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `test262_check.sh`: gate ok (exit 0; checkout at `e4fbf577`). `keycost.sh`: 278.3 M for each key (`#a1`), 283.6 M (`#f0`), peak RSS 30.9 MiB. These three JS gates run on code that this change does not touch.

Not tested: a subframe navigation (iframe) still sends no Fetch Metadata (it goes through another path); `Sec-Fetch-User` is sent only when no page started the load, so a user click that the driver makes through `act` has `same-origin` and no user flag (hypothesis: Chrome sends `?1` there); `Accept` is not Chrome's (no `image/avif`, `image/webp`, `application/signed-exchange`: bare does not decode them for a document); `accept-encoding` has no `zstd` (no decoder); the high-entropy client hints and `x-client-data` are not sent (Chrome sends them only to a server that asks for them, and `x-client-data` is a variations id of Chrome).

## Gmail PR 2 (design 2): build plan, stream the document (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): after design 1, build design 2: stream the document into the parser and start its scripts at the first bytes. This section is the plan that the owner asked for before the code. The results go in the next section when the build is measured.

### What the code does now

- A worker (`load_document`) reads the whole body (`fetch_hop` or `send_once`), decodes it (`encoding::decode`) and returns one `String`. The page thread then runs `Parsing::step`: the scan (`Scan`, the preload scanner) for half of a slice, then `tree::Parser::feed` in 16 KiB chunks. Only after the last chunk do the scripts start (`run_page`, `Run`).
- On Gmail the page thread idles 1.95 s (0.3 s to the first byte of the document and 0.77 s of body, `design-gmail-load.md` 1.2 and 1.4). The three big scripts are requested 0.03 s after the body ends.
- The loader is a pre-parsed-DOM model (header of `browser_loader.rs`): `Browser::new` takes a finished `Document`; `resources::discover` reads the whole tree once; `Run` runs the blocking scripts over a tree that is already complete. There is no half-built DOM for a script to see.

### Scope: two stages

**Stage 1 (this PR). The body streams to the scan and to the tree builder. The scripts still run when the tree is complete.**
1. Network to tokenizer. The worker reads the body in pieces (as the TLS and HTTP layers give them), decodes each piece with `encoding::Decoder` (it already exists, it is incremental, and `decode` is built on it, so the text is the same wherever the pieces are cut), and puts `Msg::Text` on a shared queue (`Feed`: `Mutex<Vec<Msg>>`). The page thread takes the queue in `Parsing::step`, appends the text to `html`, scans it and feeds the parser. Poll: the page already looks at the network every 4 ms (`Page::work`), so no wake-up channel is added.
2. Preload scan. `Scan::step` reads `html` with `more` set while the body is not over (the tokenizer stops before a cut tag, and `mark()` resumes there). The `<script src>` and `<link rel=stylesheet>` fetches start in the first slice after the first chunk. `adopt_scan` already hands these downloads to `run_page`.
3. Tree builder. `tree::Parser::feed` is already incremental: the tree is the same as `tree::parse` gives, wherever the pieces are cut (its own tests). `Parsing` is done when the body has ended and the parser has all the text; `finish` then gives the document as before.
4. A script that is blocking does not run before the tree is complete: the same semantics as today. So the order of scripts, `DOMContentLoaded` and `readyState` (`loading`, `interactive`, `complete`) are the same as today by construction. `document.write` is the existing "insert after the running script" model, unchanged.
5. Redirects, a non-HTML type, an encoded body, a download, an error status and a body that is too big are decided before the first text goes out. They keep the whole-body path (`Whole`), with the same errors and the same limits (`max_document_bytes` is counted on the bytes as they come). A body that fails in the middle is a `LoadFailed("network error")`, as before: the old document stays and no half page is shown.
6. Replay tape and virtual clock. The queue is a race between a worker thread and the page thread. The benchmark clock (`vclock`) exists to remove that kind of race (`vclock.rs` header). So streaming is off when `vclock::on()`: the journey benchmark loads the document as one task, with the due time of the task, exactly as before. The 47 journeys must show 0 change in instructions and 0 replay misses. The chunking logic is tested with fixed splits instead (a test feeds the same document in 1, 7 and 4,096 byte pieces and compares the tree and the script order with the one-piece result). A live run with a replay tape and no virtual clock is not a benchmark and may stream.
7. Memory. The worker no longer holds the body bytes and the decoded text at the same time (today: `resp.body` plus the `String`). `Parsing` keeps the decoded text until the parser has it, as today. The chunks are freed when they are moved into `html`. A document that the page left (navigation) closes the feed, and the worker stops reading at the next piece.
8. Charset. The encoding is chosen from the BOM, the header and the first 1024 bytes (`<meta charset>`), as `decode` does, because the same `Decoder` runs. Text for a cut UTF-8 letter waits in its `carry`.

**Stage 2 (not in this PR). Parser-blocking scripts that run while the body streams.** This is what Chrome does, and it is where most of the gain is: the three big scripts and their start-up code could run in the 0.8 s of the body. It needs: (a) a `Document` that the tree builder and the JS realm share, with the builder paused at a `<script>` (the builder owns its `Document`; the realm holds an `Rc<RefCell<Document>>`; the two would swap the value at each pause, and the open-element stack and the formatting list must survive a script that edits the tree); (b) an incremental `resources::discover` (today one pass over the whole tree builds `items`, `targets` and `refs` before `Run` starts, and `Run` indexes them); (c) `Run` that starts before the tree is complete, and `readyState` and `DOMContentLoaded` that wait for `finish`; (d) `document.write` that feeds the tokenizer at the insertion point instead of inserting after the script; (e) a new answer to the replay and virtual-clock rules (the point at which a chunk "arrives" must be a due time on the clock, not a thread race). That is a rewrite of the front half of `browser_loader.rs` (2,000 lines and its tests), and it changes the order of effects of every page that has a blocking script. It is not a change that fits in one PR with a safe gate. It is recorded as the next step, after Stage 1 is measured.

### How the others feed the parser

- Chrome (Blink): the network service gives the body to the renderer in pieces over a Mojo data pipe. `HTMLDocumentParser` takes them; on a worker thread (`BackgroundHTMLParser`) the tokenizer reads and a preload scanner (`HTMLPreloadScanner`) starts the fetches of scripts and styles as soon as the text is there. The tree builder runs on the main thread. A blocking script pauses the tree builder (`pending_parsing_blocking_script`); the tokenizer goes on and the preload scanner goes on; when the script is ready the builder resumes. `document.write` inserts text at the insertion point of the input stream (`InsertionPointRecord`).
- Firefox (Gecko): `nsHtml5StreamParser` receives the pieces on the network thread, decodes them (encoding chosen from BOM, header, meta prescan of the first 1024 bytes), and tokenizes on the parser thread. The tree builder emits tree operations in batches (`nsHtml5TreeOp`) to the main thread. A script stops the executor; "speculative parsing" scans ahead of a blocking script and starts its fetches; if the script's `document.write` changes the input, the speculation is thrown away.
- Servo: `html5ever` works in `ParseSink` style; the tokenizer takes `BufferQueue`, a queue of `StrTendril` pieces that the network side pushes (`ServoParser::push_string_input_chunk`). On `<script>` the tree builder returns `TokenSinkResult::Script`; the parser stops and the script runs; `document.write` pushes text in front of the `BufferQueue`. A preload scan is a later addition.
- bare after Stage 1: the same split of work as Chrome without the pause: a queue of text pieces, a preload scan that runs ahead (and that already existed), and an incremental tree builder (`Parser::feed`, with the `retry_at` rule for a long cut token). It has no pause at a script because the realm has no half-built tree. The 5 ms `Page` poll takes the place of the pipe wake-up.

### What to measure, and what to expect

Stage 1 moves the HTML parse (0.3 G, at most 0.1 s) and the start of the script fetches (the three big scripts are requested at 2.03 s, 0.03 s after the body ends, and the fetch takes 0.05 to 0.23 s to the first byte) into the wait for the body. `design-gmail-load.md` A2 estimated -0.2 s for the first row (4.4 s to 4.1 or 4.2 s, hypothesis). Instructions to the first row must not change (the same work, earlier). The big gain (4.4 s to 2.5 or 3 s, hypothesis) is in Stage 2. If Stage 1 gives -0.2 s, the owner should see that as the cost of a model that runs no script before the tree is complete.

### Tests (written first)

1. The same document in many pieces (1 byte, 7, 1,000 and 16,384 bytes, with a cut inside a UTF-8 letter, a tag, a comment and a script body) gives the same tree (serialized) as one piece.
2. A live session: the document server sends the head of the page with `<script src=/a.js>` and holds the rest until `/a.js` is requested (it gives up after 5 s). The script is requested before the last piece of the document is sent. Fails on main (the request comes after the end of the document).
3. A slow body does not delay an earlier piece: the first text and the scan are done while the server holds the rest.
4. The order of the scripts, `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` of a streamed document equals the order of the same document in one piece.
5. `document.write` in a streamed document works as in one piece. `<meta charset=windows-1252>` with a byte over 0x7F, split across pieces, gives the same text. A body over `max_document_bytes` fails as before. A body that is cut gives `LoadFailed`.
6. The virtual clock: with `BARE_CLOCK=virtual` and a tape, the document is one task (unchanged instructions in the journeys).

### Gmail PR 2 (design 2, Stage 1): result (2026-11-15)

Built as planned: the body of an HTML document streams to the scan and to the tree builder. The scripts run when the tree is complete (Stage 2 is not built; see the plan above and `decisions.md`). Code: `Feed`, `Msg`, `Loading`, `Parsing::pull`, `stream_body`, `Hop::Open` in `browser_session.rs`; `Scan::step(.., more)` with the `retry_at` rule in `browser_loader/scan.rs`. Tests (`browser_stream_tests.rs`, and two in `browser_session.rs`): a script in the first piece is requested before the last piece is sent (failed on main: `GET /a.js` came after `end`), the order of scripts, `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` and `document.write` equal one piece, windows-1252 across pieces, a body over the limit or cut short fails the load, and the saved pages give the tree of `tree::parse` when fed in pieces of 1, 7 and 5,000 bytes.

**Finding: Stage 1 does not move the Gmail first row, because the scan does not see Gmail's big scripts.** `m=b`, `m=a` and `m=ebdd,…` (`cb=loaded_0` and so on in the URL) are requested by bare right after the `DOMContentLoaded` mark (0.2 ms later), in the same round for all three, in both builds. The scan of the branch started no request for them while the body streamed, and their `wait` is 17 to 20 ms after the first script ran. So they are not static `<script src>` or stylesheet `<link>` tags of the document (hypothesis: inline code of the document adds them; to verify: read the document text, which this work did not save). Chrome runs that inline code when the parser reaches it (the request at 0.43 s, `design-gmail-load.md` 1.5). In this model no script runs before the last byte, so only Stage 2 (run the blocking inline scripts while the body streams) can use the 0.8 s of the body time, and Stage 1 cannot.

Gmail, alternating main (`81cb68d1`) and branch, 6 pairs, probe build as in #565 (`probe.patch`, not in the repository), saved session, read only. Load average 3.5 to 5.5 (first three pairs 9 s window, last three 5.5 s window):

| | main | branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First byte of the document (bimodal server wait) | 0.57, 0.77, 1.21, 1.21, 1.22, 1.23 s | 0.53, 0.57, 1.19, 1.20, 1.23, 1.24 s |
| End of the document to first row (`tr.zA`) | 2.27, 2.43, 2.45, 2.47, 2.48, 2.49 s (mean 2.43) | 2.33, 2.37, 2.42, 2.49, 2.53, 2.54 s (mean 2.45) |
| First row from `open` | 3.78, 3.81, 4.40, 4.43, 4.54, 4.63 s | 3.60, 3.81, 4.45, 4.47, 4.48, 4.60 s |
| Instructions to the first row | 16.3 to 16.9 G | 16.6 to 16.7 G |
| Peak RSS, 5.5 s window | 251, 265, 330 MiB | 242, 242, 242 MiB |
| Peak RSS, 9 s window | 331, 342, 346 MiB | 346, 354, 356 MiB |

The first row moves with the first byte of the document (the server wait), not with the change. From the end of the document it is equal: 2.43 s and 2.45 s (spread 0.2 s). Instructions are equal. The RSS rows disagree (lower in one window, higher in the other, and main alone spans 251 to 330 in one window): no claim. The scan does not start any script earlier on Gmail: in both builds the first external request after the document is the one that the inline script makes.

A page with static resources gains. Wikipedia (`Rust_(programming_language)`, 160 KB, public, 2 runs each, load 3 to 5): the stylesheet and script requests start 0.17 to 0.18 s before the end of the document on the branch, and 0.004 s after it on main. `open` took 1.19 and 0.92 s on main, 0.85 and 0.92 s on the branch: too few runs to claim a time gain.

What Stage 2 would give on Gmail (hypothesis, from the timeline above): the three big scripts are requested at the first inline script, so about 0.8 s of the body time (first byte to end of document) would hold their fetch and the start of their run. The first row would move by up to 0.8 s (4.4 s to about 3.6 s), not to the 2.5 to 3 s of the first estimate, because the JS after the document is 2.4 s (hypothesis: some of it waits on content that comes late in the document).

Checks (branch on main `81cb68d1`, archMachine, load 3 to 6):
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 4,071 passed, 7 failed, 15 ignored. The 7 are the openssl TLS tests (`https_openssl`, `client_openssl`, `tls12_openssl`), which fail on main too.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against main `81cb68d1` (803 rows): 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators and 0 under one; mean change glibc +0.007%, jemalloc +0.000%; 2 rows fail to run (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`: stack overflow, on main too).
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss` (corpus `virtual-load`): all ok, 0 replay misses; sum of median instructions 73,177.3 M base and 73,182.2 M new (+0.0%), largest spread 0.3%; sum of PSS medians 1,411.3 and 1,404.0 MiB (-0.5%). The journeys do not exercise the stream: the benchmark clock keeps the document as one task. What they show is that the one-task path did not change.
- `test262_check.sh`: gate ok (exit 0). `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh`: 278.3 M for each key (`#a1`), 283.6 M (`#f0`), peak RSS 31.1 MiB at 20 keys and 30.6 MiB at 50 keys. These three JS gates run on code that this change does not touch.

Not tested: the stream on a TLS server that sends HTTP/2 data frames of other sizes (Gmail and Wikipedia are HTTP/2, and ran); a document that redirects after a streamed `Head` (a redirect has no body, so it never streams); a navigation that leaves a document while its body still comes (the worker stops at its next read by `Arc::strong_count`; no test checks that the socket closes early); a body with a coding that the client cannot undo and a download keep the old path and have their old tests only; `document.write` and `document.open` during the stream (no script runs before the end, so they run as before); the stream under the virtual clock (off by design).

Noticed, not changed: the encoding sniff holds the first 1,024 bytes, so a first piece smaller than that is not scanned until more comes (a real first piece is 16 KiB); `Parsing` keeps the whole decoded text until the parser has it (the scan reads from an absolute offset; to free the front, both would need a rebased offset); the first inline `<script>` of Gmail could run at about 0.4 s in Chrome and runs at 2.0 s here.

## Gmail: Stage 2 check (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): verify the Stage 2 hypothesis of PR #567 before any build. This is a measurement task: no product code changed. Main `53d8809b`, archMachine, load average 2 to 8. The full result, with the structure of the document, is in [design-gmail-load.md](design-gmail-load.md) section 8. Safety as in #565 and #567: read only, bare's saved session, Chrome only through CDP on `chrome-auto` (one new tab per run, closed after, no click, no cookie copied), no account detail in any file. The saved documents and raw records are only under `/data/bare-tmp/gmail-verify/`. The scripts and the temporary probe patch are under `/data/bare-tmp/r2/gmail-verify/`.

Hypothesis: the big scripts (`m=b`, `m=a`, `m=ebdd,…`) are added by inline scripts, so bare requests them after `DOMContentLoaded` and Chrome early. Up to 0.8 s.

**Result: half right.** The effect is real; the mechanism is not inline code.
- The four URLs are in four `<link rel=preload as=script>` tags at bytes 5,807 to 6,882 of the document (the first piece). The same URLs are in `GM_JS_URLS` (inline script #1, byte 70.9 KB). Inline script #3 (bytes 126 to 202 KB) defines `_GM_loadJS`, which makes four `<script>` elements (`async = false`) and appends them to `document.body`. Inline script #7 calls it at byte 233,464 (10% of the body).
- Chrome requests the four scripts at the first byte of the document (+0.001 s, 3 cold runs), initiator `parser` (the link tags). It has no second request when `_GM_loadJS()` adds the elements. It runs them while the body streams: `_jsl` (all four ran, `_B_init` returned) is 0.60 to 0.86 s before the last byte, and the first row is 0.10 to 0.35 s before the last byte.
- bare requests them at the last byte + 0.02 s (7 runs). The scan (#567) reads only `<script src>` and stylesheet links. `preload.rs` skips the preload links of a parsed document on purpose. bare runs `_GM_loadJS()` at the last byte + 0.006 s, `_jsl` at +0.71 to +0.81 s, and the first row at +2.21 to +2.29 s.

| Big script | Source in the document | Chrome request (cold, 3 runs) and initiator | bare request (7 runs) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `m=b` | preload link (byte 5,807); `GM_JS_URLS` (70,908); `_GM_loadJS()` (233,464) | first byte +0.001 s (0.440 to 0.610 s after the request); `parser`, line 11 col 1220 | last byte +0.023 s (0.020 to 0.026) = first byte +0.76 s |
| `m=a` | preload link (6,156); `GM_JS_URLS` (71,244); `_GM_loadJS()` | first byte +0.001 s; `parser`, line 11 col 1580 | last byte +0.023 s (0.020 to 0.026) |
| `m=m,m_i` | preload link (6,516); `GM_JS_URLS` (71,601); `_GM_loadJS()` | first byte +0.001 s; `parser`, line 11 col 1946 | last byte +0.062 s (0.020 to 0.142) |
| `m=ebdd,sps,l,spit,t,it,anc` | preload link (6,882); `GM_JS_URLS` (71,964); `_GM_loadJS()` | first byte +0.001 s; `parser`, line 11 col 2337 | last byte +0.069 s (0.020 to 0.151) |

The other 45 to 58 `mail-static` scripts that Chrome loads have the initiator `script` (code inside `m=b`). They are not in the document.

Chrome with its service worker (cache on or off, 6 runs): the scripts are requested at 0.006 to 0.017 s, initiator `parser`; `_jsl` at 0.07 to 0.27 s; first row 1.03 to 1.15 s. bare has no service worker, so the cold runs are the fair comparison.

**What Stage 2 can give at most.** The loader call is at byte 233 KB, 0.23 to 0.32 s after the first byte, so the body has a window of 0.46 s (0.37 to 0.57, 7 runs) left when it runs. The CPU work to `_jsl` is 5.5 to 5.6 G instructions (0.65 s), more than the window. Before the work starts, the CPU idles 0.11 to 0.20 s after the last byte (it waits for the fetch of the scripts). The work after `_jsl` is 10.9 G (1.5 s) and does not need the late pieces of the document (Chrome's row comes before the last byte, and the data of #14 is in before `_jsl` in every bare run).

| Case | Gain on the first row (mean; range) | First row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P: request the four scripts at the first piece (a scan rule), run them as now | 0.13 s (0.09 to 0.18) | about 4.15 s |
| Stage 2 alone (scripts run while the body streams) | 0.46 s (0.37 to 0.57) | about 3.8 s |
| Stage 2 and P | 0.58 s (0.50 to 0.70) | about 3.7 s |

The hypothesis said up to 0.8 s. The bound is 0.58 s (0.50 to 0.70 s). The first row of bare stays far from Chrome's 1.2 to 1.5 s: after the scripts there are still 16.5 G of JS on one thread.

Other options (gain, complexity, risk in design section 8.7): an early runner limited to the first inline scripts has the cost and the gain of Stage 2 (inline script #7 appends to `document.body`, so the realm must see the live tree); a prefetch of URLs found in inline script text gets the same request time as P (+0.03 s) from a guess about program text, and could fetch URLs that the page never loads.

**Recommendation: build option P (the preload rule in the scan, about 6 lines and two tests, 0.13 s). Do not build Stage 2 now.** Stage 2 gives at most 0.58 s (13.5%) on one page class (a long body and an early blocking script). It is a rewrite of the front half of the loader that changes the order of effects of every page, and the 47 journeys (virtual clock) cannot show its gain. If the owner wants it, the order is: P, then the JS work, then Stage 2. The window stays about 0.4 to 0.6 s when JS gets faster, so its share of the first row grows. The owner decides.

Method. A probe build of main `53d8809b` with the #565 probe and a dump of each decoded piece of the document with its arrival time (`/data/bare-tmp/r2/gmail-verify/probe-full.patch`, own target dir `/data/bare-tmp/target-gmail-verify`). bare: 7 runs of one fresh `bare-mcp`, `open` with the saved session; 4 runs with the first-row probe (`tr.zA`), 3 with a probe on `window._jsl === true`; `perf stat -I 100` for instructions; request times from `BARE_NET_TRACE`. Chrome 155 through CDP: `Network.requestWillBeSent` (initiator), `Network.dataReceived` (arrival of decoded bytes), `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` (a setter on `_jsl`, a `MutationObserver` for the first `tr.zA`, `PerformanceResourceTiming` initiator types). 9 runs: cache off with the service worker bypassed (3), cache off (3), cache on (3). The document structure comes from the saved text of one bare run and one cold Chrome run (same offsets for the first 233 KB).

Checks: none to run (docs only). The scripts were run on the numbers above. Each run closed its tab (`Target.closeTarget`); after the 9 runs the target list has the same 8 entries as before them. A Gmail `service_worker` target showed up once during the runs and went away.

Not tested: Stage 2 and P themselves (nothing was built); the gain is the measured window and idle gap, not a run. The idle gap has 0.05 s of error (100 ms bins). A slow network, another account, a larger mailbox. The split of the 0.65 s of work to `_jsl` (fetch decode, top-level run, `_B_init`). Whether a page that needs the last piece of the document would get less.

Noticed, not changed:
- `m=m,m_i` and `ebdd` are requested 0.02 to 0.15 s after `m=b` and `m=a` in 3 of 7 bare runs, in the same round as `_GM_loadJS()` in the other 4 (hypothesis: a limit of the worker slots in `Net`). P would hide it.
- `preload.rs` says that a fetch for the preload links of a parsed document "would only cost time and memory" because bare has no HTTP cache. That is true for a link that no script uses, and false for a link whose URL a script takes later, as here. P must keep the first case from costing anything: check that an unused scan download does not hold `Page::pending`.

## Gmail: the preload rule in the scan (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): build option P of [design-gmail-load.md](design-gmail-load.md) section 8 (a preload rule in the scan). Do not build Stage 2. Recorded in `decisions.md`.

**What was built.** `Scan::start` (`browser_loader/scan.rs`) now starts a download for `<link rel=preload as=script href>` and for `<link rel=preload as=style href>`. It is the same few lines for both kinds, so both are built. The download is a hint: it has the key of a `<script src>` or a stylesheet link (`Net::key(kind, url)`), so the element that the page code adds later takes it (`Net::fetch`), and the element makes no second request. Gmail names its four big scripts in such links at bytes 5,807 to 6,882 of a 2.3 MB document, and `_GM_loadJS()` adds the elements at byte 233,464.

What `preload.rs` protected, and how it stays protected.
- "A browser fires their events before any script can listen": the scan fires no event. `preload.rs` still skips the parsed links in the style pass, so a parsed link gets no `load` and no second fetch.
- "bare has no HTTP cache, so a fetch would only cost time and memory": true for a link that no element takes. Such a hint (a) holds no page work: `Net::hints` marks it, and `waiting_loads` (`Page::pending`) says `holds = false` for it before `load` and after it, until an element names the same URL (the scan then clears the mark, and `Net::fetch` clears it when the file is taken); (b) delays no `load`, because `load` never waited for a download that no element took; (c) keeps its text under the same caps as any scan download (`WINDOW` of 32, `max_fetches`, `max_total_bytes` through `done`), and a page that ends drops it (`Drop for Net`). Fonts, images and the other `as` values start nothing (the staging login has four font preloads).
- Credentials mode. bare has one mode for scripts and sheets (no CORS mode; `crossorigin` is "Not done" in `preload.rs`, `sheets.rs` and `modules.rs`). A link with `crossorigin` has another mode than a script without it. So it starts nothing, and the script requests its own file. A link without `crossorigin` has the mode of a script without it, so the URL and that mode match. Not done: a link and a script that both have `crossorigin` (Chrome reuses the response, bare requests it at the script). `integrity`: bare checks none, so a reused response cannot differ in effect. Not done: a script with `crossorigin` taking a hint without it (bare does not model the mismatch).
- A hint that comes before a `<base href>` resolves against the page, as a `<script src>` does: its download is then not used (a second request, as before).

Tests (written first; `browser_stream_tests.rs`). Before the change 3 of 5 failed:
1. A preload link in the first piece, the script added later by an inline script: one request, started before the document ends (log order `GET /a.js` before `piece 1`), and the script runs. Failed on main (`GET /a.js` after `end`).
2. A link with `crossorigin`: the script requests its own file once, after the end of the document (passes on main and after: it guards the rule).
3. A hint that no script takes (`/a.js` answers 3 s late): `load` is not delayed (page loaded in under 2.5 s), and the inline script of the page ran. Failed on main (no request at all).
4. `Page::pending` before `load` (a scan adopted by a page that has not loaded): the hint has `holds = false`; with a `<script src>` of the same URL before or after it, `holds = true`. I checked that this test fails when the rule is removed. (The test above cannot show it alone: after `load`, `holds` is false anyway.)
5. A style preload and a stylesheet link added later: one request, before the end of the document. Failed on main.

**Gmail measurement.** Saved session, read only, no click. `bare-mcp` probe builds as in #569 (`probe-full.patch`, not in the repository): newest main `2211c276` and this branch, each in its own target dir, 5 alternating pairs, 9 s window, machine load 12 down to 3.8 (pair 1 ran at load 12). No account detail is written here. Raw output is under `/data/bare-tmp/gmail-preload-runs/` (it holds session URLs).

| Run (base, new) | First byte of the document | End of the document to first row | First row from `open` | Instructions to first row |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.61, 0.53 s | 3.00, 2.21 s (load 12) | 4.49, 3.57 s | 16.7, 17.0 G |
| 2 | 1.23, 0.48 s | 2.27, 2.23 s | 4.35, 3.49 s | 16.8, 16.9 G |
| 3 | 0.55, 0.52 s | 2.35, 2.17 s | 3.70, 3.48 s | 16.6, 16.8 G |
| 4 | 1.14, 1.17 s | 2.26, 2.16 s | 4.31, 4.16 s | 16.7, 16.9 G |
| 5 | 1.11, 1.14 s | 2.33, 2.21 s | 4.19, 4.10 s | 17.0, 17.0 G |
| Median | | 2.33, 2.21 s | 4.31, 3.57 s | 16.7, 16.9 G |

The first byte of the document is bimodal (0.5 or 1.1 to 1.2 s: the server wait) and dominates "from `open`". So the fair numbers are the pairs with the same first byte, and the time from the end of the document. Pairs 3, 4, 5 (same first-byte mode): first row 0.22, 0.15 and 0.09 s earlier (mean 0.15 s). End of document to first row: median 2.33 to 2.21 s (-0.12 s); excluding run 1 (load 12) the base range is 2.26 to 2.35 s and the new range 2.16 to 2.23 s. The design estimate was 0.13 s (0.09 to 0.18). Pair 2 (first byte 1.23 against 0.48 s) is not a pair of equal conditions: its 0.86 s is the server wait, not the change.

Request time of the four big scripts, seconds after the first byte of the document:

| | `m=b` | `m=a` | `m=m,m_i` | `m=ebdd,…` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| main (5 runs) | 0.77 to 0.93 | 0.77 to 0.93 | 0.82 to 1.01 | 0.88 to 1.02 |
| branch (5 runs) | 0.006 to 0.017 | 0.006 to 0.017 | 0.006 to 0.017 | 0.006 to 0.017 |

On the branch all four are requested in the same instant, at the first piece (Chrome: +0.001 s). On main they come 0.02 s after the last byte (0.77 s to 1.02 s after the first byte); in 3 of 5 runs `m=m,m_i` and `ebdd` started 0.08 to 0.15 s after `m=b` and `m=a`. Peak RSS (VmHWM) 333 to 363 MiB on main (mean 346) and 340 to 369 MiB on the branch (mean 353): the spread of one build (30 MiB) is larger than the difference, so no claim. The four scripts are about 5 MB of text and now wait in `started` for 0.8 s longer (hypothesis: that is the +7 MiB; not measured apart).

The late starts of two scripts on main (3 of 5 runs here, 3 of 7 in #569). The hypothesis of #569 was a limit of the worker slots. That is not it: `MAX_WORKERS` is 6, and four downloads need 4. On the branch the four start at once in 5 of 5 runs, so the case does not appear on a page that names its scripts in preload links. The cause on a page that does not is not found (hypothesis: `Run::prefetch` returns early while `Client::parallel_pays()` is false, so the page thread fetches the later scripts itself, one at a time; to verify). Not changed.

**Checks** (branch `9b336c91` on main `2211c276`, archMachine, `bin/heavy` was missing for the later checks, see below; the machine had no other build running, load 2 to 6).

The 9 new and old `browser_stream_tests` pass.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against main `2211c276` (built with `--workspace --examples -p bare-stress`, then `-p bare-drive -p bare-stress`): 803 rows, 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators, 0 under one; mean change glibc -0.000%, jemalloc +0.000%; 2 rows fail to run (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`: stack overflow, on main too).
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`: all ok, 0 replay misses ("none"); sum of median instructions 73,188.4 M base and 73,192.9 M new (+0.0%; the largest change is +0.2% on `httpbin-form-fill`, 0.05 M), largest spread 0.3%. A hint that a journey did not take would show as a replay miss or as more instructions: there are none, so (hypothesis, not checked per page) no journey has an unused script or sheet preload. The PSS sum and the peak-RSS column disagree (PSS -8.0%, peak RSS +0.4%): no claim on memory from the journeys.
- `test262_check.sh`: gate ok (exit 0). `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh`: 278.3 M for each key (`#a1`), 283.6 M (`#f0`), peak RSS 30.7 MiB at 20 keys and 31.0 MiB at 50 keys. These three run on code that this change does not touch.

**Not tested.**
- A preload link of a page that is not Gmail on the live web (the 47 journeys have none for a script or sheet that they do not use, so the cost of an unused hint is only tested with a stalled file, not measured on a real page).

## Gmail JS cost: design (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): design how to cut the JS cost of Gmail. No build yet. Task R2-J. Design: `docs/design-gmail-js.md`.

**Method.** Main `2211c276`. Release build with symbols and frame pointers. Gmail inbox, saved bare session, read only (no click, no input, no login). Machine archMachine, load average 3 to 7. Plain build: `perf stat` 3 runs and `perf record` 1 run. Counting build: 1 run (counts do not vary). Instruction build with a per-call counter: 3 runs (first row agrees to 0.3%). The counter adds 13% at the first row, so shares are exact and sizes are low by that factor. Raw data stays under `/data/bare-tmp/r2/gmail-js/raw/`. `/data/bare-tmp/bin/` was gone during the work; a private copy of `heavy` with the same lock was used.

**Result (first row, 17.3 G; settle 103 to 116 G, mean 107.6 G, 3 runs).**

| Item | First row | Settle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JS interpreter | 69.8% | 77.0% |
| JS parse (top parse 1.5 G, lazy load 1.1 G, instrumented) | 13.8% | 4.7% |
| allocator | 4.7% | 4.4% |
| bindings | 2.1% | 4.7% |
| style | 2.0% | 3.4% |
| tree-walk dispatch functions (`link_inner`, `eval_expr_inner`, `exec_simple`, `exec_list`, `machine`, `test_true`, `eval_assign`, `link_base`) | 30% | 31% |
| calls (dispatch 168, select 127, setup 221, teardown 82, return 55 = 653 per frame call; 839 per env call) | 10.5% | 11.7% |

- 50.75 M steps and 3.06 M calls to the first row (268 instructions per step inside functions). 2.92 M script calls: 2.10 M frame path, 0.82 M env path. 0.59 M native calls. 12 K host calls.
- 41% of the object member reads refill the one-entry cache (2.25 M of 5.49 M). 919 sites cause 84% of the refills. `get_dict` + `lookup` + `PropMap::find` cost 4.5%. The `IC_DICT` entry names one object (`heap_shape.rs:1119`). Hypothesis: dictionary receivers are most of the refills (step 1 of design P2 counts it).
- 365 functions with 1,000 or more calls take 68% of function self (41% of the thread). 5,021 functions run once (0.55 G). Cold cost (parse and first run) is 3.3 G.
- A one-step function costs 702 instructions per call.
- Natives are 4%. Host calls are 6%, mostly forced layout (`clientWidth` 13 calls 457 M).
- The byte lane runs 5% of the calls (lazy functions are refused). It gives nothing on Gmail today (18.3 G against 17.7 G at the first row, 1 run).
- The cost is flat: the top JS function is 5.7% of function self, the top 20 are 38%.

**Designs, ranked** (`design-gmail-js.md` sections 5 to 7). Gains are hypotheses (nothing was built).

| Rank | Design | Gain, first row | Work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | P1 parse a script on arrival, on a worker (the body download leaves 0.46 s idle) | page thread -1.4 G (-8%), about -0.3 s | S to M |
| 2 | P4 `ErrorCtor` (3.8 M per call), `Paren` nodes | -0.1 to -0.4 G | XS |
| 3 | P2 dictionary position hint, then a shared stub cache | -0.3 to -0.6 G (2 to 3.5%) | S |
| 4 | P3 call path: callee index in the function object, one `ScriptCtx` pointer, arguments into frame slots | -0.8 to -1.1 G (5 to 6%) | M |
| 5 | P5 disk cache of parse results | repeat visit -2.0 G (-0.9 G after P1) | L |
| 6 | P6 hot tier (finish the bytecode lane: lazy functions, shared ICs, 100 calls) | -3.5 to -4.2 G (-20 to -24%) at 2.0x to 2.49x | L to XL |

P1 to P4 together: -3 G (-18%), first row about 3.5 s (now 4.15 s). With P6: about 2.6 to 2.8 s. Chrome: 1.2 to 1.5 s. A byte-code tier does not close the gap. Only a baseline JIT can, and it is not proposed.

**Recommendation (the owner decides).** Build P1 and P4 first, with the step 1 count of P2. Then P3. Decide on P6 after P3, because P3 is a part of P6.

**Not tested.** Nothing was built or timed in wall clock. The gains are instruction counts, with time at an assumed 4 to 5 G per second. Not measured: the dictionary share of refills, arguments objects, scope-depth lookups, why 28% of the calls take the env path, memory, other accounts, the 47 journeys, the cost matrix. Main moved to `c73dc3c3` (#570, the preload rule) after the measurement; the window for P1 is the one measured in #569 (0.46 s) and needs a new check on the new main.

Noticed, not changed:
- `<&str as Pattern>::is_contained_in` is 2.5% after the first row (about 2.2 G at settle). It is in the bindings or style path. Not JS.
- `get clientWidth` costs 4.79 G at settle (91 calls). This is forced layout, not JS.
- `Program` holds `Rc` in `ast.rs` (lines 584, 604, 635, 637), so it is not `Send`. P1 needs a hand-over wrapper, and P5 needs relocatable arenas.

## Gmail P2: a dictionary read hits at any position (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): build P1, P4 and P2 of `design-gmail-js.md` now in parallel, then P3; decide on P6 (bytecode) after P3. This section is P2.

**Step 1: the count.** A probe build (not committed; diff and counters in `/data/bare-tmp/r2/p2/`) classified every member read that left the inline hit. Main `ca67571d`, Gmail inbox, saved bare session, read only. First row, 2 runs (agree to 0.3%); settle, 1 run.

| | First row | Settle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow reads (out of the inline hit) | 3.41 M | 26.2 M |
| Chain hits (prototype method, absent key): not misses | 0.99 M | 6.3 M |
| Misses on a dictionary receiver | 2.06 M (91% of misses) | 17.8 M (91%) |
| Misses on a shaped receiver | 0.22 M | 1.76 M |
| Dictionary misses with the key at position 256 or more | 99.4% | 99.6% |
| Dictionary misses on the same object as the last read at the site | 99% | 99.5% |
| Dictionary misses that the position hint of the design would hit (another object, same position) | 4.4 K | 16 K |
| Shaped misses that a 4-shape entry or a 4,096-entry stub table would hit (simulated) | 0.13 M | 1.3 M |

The gate (dictionary refills more than half) is met, but the cause is different from the design guess. The `IC_DICT` entry held the key position in a `u8`. A dictionary of 256 or more keys never got an entry, so every read of it took `get_dict` and a hash lookup. The design's position hint (read another object at the same position) hits 0.2% of the reads: not built. A polymorphic entry or a stub table would remove 0.13 M refills (about 45 M instructions, 0.3%): not built, it does not pay for the memory.

**Built.** `Ic::depth` is a `u16`. An `IC_DICT` entry holds a position up to 65,535. `Ic` stays 24 bytes (test `an_entry_is_24_bytes_and_the_empty_entry_never_hits` in `heap_shape.rs`; `depth`, `kind` and `misses` share 4 bytes). 14 lines of code. Memory per site: no change.

**Tests (written first, the counter test failed before the change).** `a_site_that_reads_a_dictionary_of_over_255_keys_hits_inline` (100 reads, 100 inline hits, 0 fills). Case `big_dict` in `eval_ic_tests.rs` (expected text from Node 22): a 600-key dictionary read at one site through a write, a delete, a re-add, 100 deletes, 100 adds (positions move), a getter, a read-only data property, `Object.freeze`, a second object with the key at another position, and a chain of prototypes with a shadow, a delete and a prototype swap. The debug build checks every hit against the plain walk (`ic_verify`): the `ic_tests` pass there too.

**Numbers, Gmail** (plain build of main `ca67571d` and of the branch, with one measurement patch on both that reads the page-thread instruction counter at the first row; 5 pairs, alternating, load average 3.5 to 16 from other agents). Instructions on the page thread from the page start to the first row (`tr.zA` present):

| | base | new |
| --- | --- | --- |
| median | 16.424 G | 15.681 G |
| range | 16.254 to 16.430 | 15.612 to 15.701 |

Change: -0.743 G (-4.5%). The design hypothesis was -0.3 to -0.6 G. Slow reads at the first row fall from 3.41 M to 1.35 M; dictionary misses from 2.06 M to 25 K. At settle the counter gives 79 to 110 G in both builds (the settle point moves from run to run), so no claim on settle: the probe build shows slow reads from 26.2 M to 7.6 M (1 run each). Wall time: the time from the end of the document to the first row is 2.0 to 5.6 s in the new build and 2.1 to 2.7 s in the base build under that load: no claim (the document end moved 1.5 to 2.4 s: the first byte is bimodal; not paired by mode).

**Checks.**
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 4,076 pass, 8 fail: the 7 openssl TLS tests (known on main) and `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` (known flaky).
- `cost_matrix.sh` against main `ca67571d` (built with `--workspace --examples -p bare-stress`, then `-p bare-drive -p bare-stress`): 803 rows, 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators, 0 under one; mean glibc +0.001%, jemalloc +0.000%; 2 rows fail to run (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`, stack overflow, as on main).
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`: all ok, 0 replay misses; sum of median instructions 73,191.0 M base and 73,192.7 M new (+0.0%, largest journey change +0.2% spread). No journey reads a dictionary of 256 or more keys often enough to move.
- `test262_check.sh`: gate ok (exit 0). `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh`: 278.3 M for each key (`#a1`), 283.6 M (`#f0`), peak RSS 30.9 MiB at 20 keys and 31.0 MiB at 50 keys (same as before: the typing page has no big dictionary).

**Not tested.**
- Peak RSS of Gmail (the entry is 24 bytes as before; no new table).
- A dictionary of more than 65,535 keys (the entry is not filled; the read takes the old path).
- The bytecode lane (it has its own entries).
- Gmail with another account or a warm cache.
- Which object is the big dictionary (hypothesis: a namespace object of a few thousand keys).

Noticed, not changed.
- 0.99 M reads at the first row (6.3 M at settle) are chain hits (a method on the prototype, an absent key). They leave the inline `ic_own` and go through `member_ic` and `get_ic` each time. A second inline test for the prototype kind could remove the call and the stats update (hypothesis; not measured).
