## Gmail P4: the cost of an error and the Paren node (2026-11-15)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): build P1, P4 and P2 of `design-gmail-js.md` now in parallel (three agents, separate code), then P3; decide on P6 (bytecode) after P3. This section is P4. Decision record: `decisions.md`, design: `design-gmail-js.md` (P4, "Result").

**What the cost of an error was.** `ErrorCtor` took 3.8 M instructions per call on the Gmail first row. The cause is not the work of one error. The first position lookup in a script makes the location marks of the whole script (`lex::location_marks`, one pass at 19 instructions per byte). A 1.5 MB one-line script: 28.6 M for the marks, then 54 K for each later error (a scan of up to 4 KiB). A small script: 20 K for each error. Gmail has three scripts of 4.9 MB in all. The lazy `stack` text (V8) would remove the work, but the work is now small (see below), so it is not built.

**Built.**
1. `lex::scan` reads 32 bytes in one pass when the block has no CR (13) and no E2 byte (a possible LS or PS). The pass counts LF, the units, and sets a flag for the two special bytes; a block with one of them takes the byte loop as before. A block with LF takes the units after the last LF. 1.5 MB marks: 28.6 M to 3.0 M (9.6 times fewer, 2 instructions per byte). I tried 16 and 64 bytes and three passes over the block: slower or equal.
2. `ExprKind::Paren` is removed. `parse_paren` returns the inner expression. The parser keeps `parens`, the sorted ids of the expressions that were in parentheses (an expression gets its id after its parts, so the list is sorted without a sort; `arena_truncate` cuts it back for a dropped lazy body). It is asked in: `pattern_of` (a target in parentheses is a name or a member only, and no binding), `is_arrow`, the directive and the label of an expression statement, `**` after a unary or `await`, `??` beside `&&` or `||`, `for ((async) of`, and the flag of `export default (function () {})`. `StmtKind::ExportDefault(e, bool)`: true when the function is not in parentheses (it is made at instantiation). The evaluator and the bytecode generator lost their `Paren` arms and `unparen`/`strip` helpers.

**Tests (written first, they passed on the old code and still pass).** `parse::tests::parentheses_keep_their_meaning`: 143 texts, each with the status that Node gives (accept or reject). `eval::paren_tests`: 64 scripts with the value that Node gives (the `this` of `(o.f)()`, `(o?.f)()`, `((o.f))()`, tagged templates and `with`-less cases; `(o?.b).c` and `(o?.b)()` on null; `delete`; `typeof (nope)`; name inference through parentheses and `(0, f)`; `toString` text; targets of `=`, `+=`, `++`, destructuring and `for ((a) of`; `**`; `??`; arrows; directives; `new (o.C)`), and the stack position of a call with a parenthesized callee (`(g)()`, `((g))()`, `(o.g)()`, `(o?.g)()`, `(0, g)()`, `(g)\`x\``, `( g )( )`). `lex::tests::marked_locations_match_the_reference_on_random_text`: 6 random texts of 8 KB with runs of plain text, CR, LF, CRLF, LS, PS, E2 and wide characters, every offset compared with the character reference. After the change test262 found one more case (`language/module-code/instn-named-bndng-dflt-expr`, `export default (function () {})` was hoisted); `a_default_function_in_parentheses_is_made_when_its_statement_runs` covers it.

**Numbers, Gmail first row** (saved bare session, read only, no click; probe builds that read the page-thread instruction counter, on main `5b0b76b1` and on the branch; 7 alternating pairs; load average 1 to 4; the raw output holds session URLs and stays under `/data/bare-tmp/r2/p4/raw/`):

| | base | new |
| --- | --- | --- |
| page-thread instructions to the first row, median | 15.509 G | 15.344 G (-0.165 G, -1.1%) |
| range of the 7 runs | 15.153 to 15.675 | 14.969 to 15.505 |
| `Error` construction at the first row (19 to 28 calls) | 102.7 to 112.4 M | 13.0 to 14.7 M (-87%) |

An earlier build of the scan (3 passes) gave 30 M for the errors and -0.156 G (median 15.673 to 15.517, 7 pairs). The error probe explains -95.5 M of the -0.165 G; the rest (-70 M) fits 1.13 M evaluations of `Paren` at about 64 instructions each (hypothesis: not counted on its own in Gmail). A synthetic loop with 9 parentheses in each pass: 7,430 to 6,850 instructions for each pass (-7.8%, `paren_cost`, 200,000 passes, not committed). The first row moves from run to run by 0.5 G (the first byte of the document is bimodal), so the gain is a median of 7 pairs, not a claim for one run. Settle: not measured (the settle point moves from run to run, as in P2).

**Checks.**
- `cost_matrix.sh` against main `5b0b76b1` (built with `--workspace --examples`, then `-p bare-drive -p bare-stress`): 803 rows, 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators; mean glibc -0.275%, jemalloc +0.007%; 1 noise candidate (`loader_load blocking 10`: glibc +0.62%, jemalloc +0.01%); 2 rows fail to run (`parse_load deep 1` and `10`, stack overflow, as on main). The best rows: `date_load utc` -4.5%, `parse_load malformed` -3.0%, `eval_load throws` -2.6% (errors with positions).
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`: all ok, 0 replay misses; sum of median instructions 73,189.0 M base and 72,677.7 M new (-0.7%, spread 0.2% at most); the largest: `wiktionary-portal` -2.4%, `wikipedia-portal` -2.0%, `wikipedia-main-random` -1.7%, `github-docs-home` -1.3%. cpu_ms -0.7%, wall_ms -0.8%, PSS sum -0.6%. Single PSS rows move by up to 7% (a sample every 20 ms): `devto-home` and `wikipedia-article` rerun with 7 runs: +1.3% and -3.6%, instructions equal.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 4,080 pass, 9 fail: the 7 openssl TLS tests (known on main) and `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` and `a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero` (known flaky under load). `bare-js` alone: 985 pass.
- `test262_check.sh`: gate ok; the result of each of the 32,838 tests is the same as with the runner of main `ca67571d` (`diff` of `results.txt` is empty). The baseline file is older than main: the gate also prints many "newly passing" directories on main; this change does not update it. `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh`: 276.9 M for each key (`#a1`), 282.2 M (`#f0`), peak RSS 31.0 and 30.9 MiB; main gives the same.
- Parser output of main against the branch (`parse_check cases` on the 2,207 cases, after the error text is normalized): every accepted tree and span is the same; 13 rejected cases differ in the text and the column of the error only (the inner expression has no parentheses in its span). `parse_check dump` of 13 real script files: 0 differences. This is not a comparison with Acorn: the pinned Acorn is 8.15.0 and `parse_check.sh` was not run.

**Limits.** None removed. The step charge of the first location lookup in a script (1 step for 32 bytes) is now higher than the work; it is left. `Limits::max_nodes` counts one node fewer for each parenthesis, so a script near the cap parses with a little room.

**Not tested.**
- The cost matrix, the journeys, `cargo test --workspace`, `keycost.sh` and the Gmail numbers ran before the last commit (the span of a parenthesized sequence: one `mk_expr_at` call changed). After it, `bare-js` tests (986), `exec_diff.sh` (0 differences) and `test262_check.sh` (gate ok, results equal to main) ran again.
- Settle of Gmail, peak RSS of Gmail, Gmail with another account or a warm cache.
- Wall time of the first row (load 1 to 6 from other agents; the first byte is bimodal).
- Another architecture: the block loop is plain Rust and the compiler makes vectors from it; only x86-64 was measured.
- A script with many LS or PS characters in its first 32-byte blocks (they take the byte loop; correct by test, not measured).
- The bytecode lane: it has no `Paren` arms any more and `exec_diff` shows no difference, but it runs 5% of the Gmail calls.

**Noticed, not changed.**
- Three differences from V8 that the tests found on the old code too: `with (o) { (f)() }` calls `f` with the global as `this` (V8: `o`); `delete (o?.p)` does not delete (V8 does); `010` gives 10 in a sloppy function (V8: 8). The tests leave them out.
- `(a) = function () {}` names the function `a` (spec: it does not, `(a)` is not an identifier reference). Main does the same: test262 `language/expressions/assignment/fn-name-lhs-cover.js` fails in both runs.
- `export default () => 1` is made when the module is instantiated, as a declaration is (spec: when the statement runs). Main does the same: its check is `ExprKind::Function(_)`, as is the new flag (read from the code; no test run).
- `keycost.sh` and every other script that builds with `cargo` use the current directory and `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Run from a worktree with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` set to a `base-build` directory, it builds the worktree's source into the base. That happened once during this work (`examples/type_load` of `5b0b76b124` was replaced); it was restored from the original build output (`type_load-fe82c79384938f3a`). Run the script of the base from its own `src` directory.

## Gmail P1: parse a script on a worker thread (2026-11-15)

**Built.** A classic script that a document names is parsed on one worker thread when its text arrives (`crates/js/src/parse_ahead.rs`). The download thread hands the text to the worker, as one `Rc<str>` that the tree keeps afterwards (no second copy). `parse_cache::parse` calls `parse_ahead::take`. A text that the worker has not begun is parsed by the page thread; a text that the worker runs is waited for; a finished tree is taken after a byte compare and a node-room check. A syntax error is stored in the result and reported by the run at the same place as before. A navigation (`Ahead::cancel`) closes the worker, drops the finished trees and marks the queued texts gone. A running parse is not interrupted. The worker ends 2 s after its last text. Design and decision: [design-gmail-js.md](design-gmail-js.md), [decisions.md](decisions.md).

Scope, chosen from the journey numbers: only scripts that the document names (scan scripts, `as=script` preloads) and that no cache holds (`parse_cache::known`). A dynamic script is not parsed ahead: the first build did it and the 47 journeys paid more instructions for texts that no run needed.

Replay under the virtual clock: the worker is not a `parallel::Task`, reads no `bare_net` clock, and the page thread waits in real time. The tree is a pure function of (text, kind, limits), so the replay is the same with and without the worker. 0 replay misses.

**Idle window re-check (main `c73dc3c3` or later).** The idle window that P1 uses is 0.61 to 0.75 s on the newest main, so it exists (it is larger than the design counted).

**Numbers (Gmail first row; machine archMachine, 5 runs each in 2 rounds, load average 3.0 to 8.2, probe build for the per-thread counter).** Page-thread instructions to the first row:

| build | page thread to first row | whole process to first row |
|---|---|---|
| main `5b0b76b1` | 16.42 G (16.25 to 16.45 in 10 runs) | 17.0 G |
| this change | 14.9 to 15.2 G (10 runs) | 16.4 to 17.1 G |

The page thread is 1.2 to 1.5 G lower (-8% to -9%). The whole process is not lower: the work moved to the worker. The expected -1.4 G holds. The first byte of the server is bimodal (0.5 s or 1.1 s), so the first-row times are compared inside one mode. First byte 0.5 s: main 3.42, 3.57, 3.65 s; this change 3.44, 3.46, 3.47 s (-0.1 s). First byte 1.1 s: main 4.05, 4.17 s; this change 4.03, 4.07 s. The saving in wall time is about 0.1 s, not the expected 0.3 s (the first row waits for other work too). Peak RSS (VmHWM) is 339 to 379 MiB in main and 339 to 368 MiB in this change: no change.

**Checks.**
- New tests (they fail without `take`): same results and errors with and without the worker, a parse that ends after the page needs it, a navigation that drops pending parses, a syntax error at the right place, and 2 browser stream tests. 11 unit tests in `parse_ahead.rs`.
- `cargo test --release --workspace`: only the known failures (the 7 openssl TLS tests; one flaky test of the known list in one run).
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`: all ok, 0 replay misses; sum of median instructions 73,190 M main and 73,295 M this change (+0.1%, largest journey +0.2%); CPU time +0.5%, wall time -0.5%, PSS -1.0% (under load).
- `test262_check.sh`: gate ok (exit 0). `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh`: 278.3 M (`#a1`), 283.6 M (`#f0`), as before.
- Cost matrix, 803 rows (2 fail to run as on main: `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`): **the gate does not pass: 4 rows are over +0.5% under both allocators.** `builtins_load replace 1` (+1.20%), `replace 10` (+1.36%), `scan 1` (+1.03%), `scan 10` (+1.15%) against main built in the same worktree path; mean glibc +0.025%. The rows run no code of this change in their loop. The sampled difference is in `Regex::exec_in` (-38 samples) and in `builtins_load::run` (a `Vec::from_iter` that was inlined in main is a call here: +25 samples). Hypothesis: a different inlining choice from the added code in the crate, as in the cost-of-frame-slots entry. Moving the cache-miss code of `parse` into a cold function gave the same counts, so it is not that code.
- A matrix against the shared base build `base-build origin/main` shows 91 rows over (worst `date_load utc` +4.7%). That is a difference of build environment: main built in this worktree gives the same +4.7% against the shared base. The base for the matrix of a branch must be built in the same path as the branch.

**Not tested.**
- Gmail with another account or a warm cache.
- A parse that the worker runs while a second window navigates (one worker, one registry for all pages).
- Wall time of the first row on an idle machine (load average above 3 in all runs).
- Modules and dynamic scripts (not parsed ahead by design; they take the old path).

### Gmail P1 after the rebase: the 4 cost rows (2026-11-15, main `d710aa97`)

Owner decision (2026-11-15): rebase P1 on the newest main, run the gates again, and try to bring the 4 cost rows back. The rebase had no conflict (#574 touched other lines). Result: **the 4 rows stay over. The branch is pushed and the PR is open, not merged.**

**Method.** Main and the branch were built in this one worktree path (the same path depth and layout), into two target dirs, once with `--release --workspace --examples` and once with `--release -p bare-drive -p bare-stress`. The shared `base-build` was not used for the matrix.

**Gates (rebased branch, machine archMachine).**
- Cost matrix, 803 rows: the same 4 rows are over under both allocators: `builtins_load replace 1` +0.99%, `replace 10` +1.15%, `scan 1` +0.85%, `scan 10` +0.97% (glibc). Mean glibc change +0.011%. No other row. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` fail to run, as on main.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: only known failures (the 7 openssl TLS tests; `a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero`, `external_sheets_embedded_sheets_and_inline_styles_cascade_in_order`, `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved`: a different one of these 3 flaky tests fails in each run).
- test262: gate ok. `exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. `keycost.sh`: 276.9 M (`#a1`), 282.2 M (`#f0`), peak RSS 30.8 MiB at 50 keys.
- 47 journeys, `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`: all ok, 0 replay misses. Sum of median instructions 72,675 M main, 72,776 M branch (+0.1%; largest `react-docs` +0.4%, `rust-book-search` +0.4%). CPU time +0.8%, wall time +0.1% (the machine was loaded), PSS -8.7% (noise: one run of `devto-home` and others move PSS by several MiB).

**Gmail (saved session, read only, no click; probe builds that read the page-thread counter; 6 alternating pairs; load average 4.7 to 10).** Page-thread instructions to the first row: main 15.34, 15.51, 15.50, 15.50, 15.34, 15.51 G (median 15.50 G); branch 14.12, 14.27, 14.27, 14.10, 14.20, 14.11 G (median 14.16 G). That is -1.3 G (-8.6%) on the page thread. Time from the start of the load to the first row: main 1.96 to 2.51 s (median 2.11 s), branch 1.92 to 2.18 s (median 2.06 s). The load was too high and the first-byte mode was not recorded for these runs, so the time is not a claim. Settle and peak RSS: not measured again.

**Cause of the 4 rows (measured; the fix is not found).**
- All 4 rows are `builtins_load` and run `Regex::exec_in`. Callgrind (`replace 1`): the call lists and the call counts of `exec_in` are the same in both builds. Its own instructions are 18.52 M in main and 19.12 M in the branch (+0.60 M). `replace 1` runs 633,974 regexp steps, so it is 1 instruction for each step.
- The disassembly shows it: in main the dispatch loop keeps the address of the jump table in a callee-saved register. In the branch the compiler makes that address (`lea`) again at each step. The rest is a different choice of registers. No inlining changed.
- The cause is the choice of the codegen units. `-Z print-mono-items` shows that the CGU of `regexp` is merged with the `alloc` instances in main and with the `std` instances in the branch. With `-C codegen-units=1`, main and the branch are the same: `replace 1` 62,696,254 and 62,696,564. (That is 1.9% above main with 16 units, so main has the good layout by luck.)
- Narrow builds (`-p bare-js --example builtins_load`, same path, `replace 1`): main 61,533,963 to 61,534,392; the branch 62,143,846. Main plus only `pub(crate) hash` and the `parse_raw` split: 61,533,963 (no change). Main plus the `take` call and the node-room code, without the registry of keys: 61,534,141 (no change). The calls of the cache to the registry of keys (`remember` on insert, `forget` on evict, `new_realm` and `clear`) bring the +1.0%, in each form that was tried. The `parse_ahead` module is not needed for it (the same +1.0% when the module is left out, and when its code is inside `parse_cache.rs`).
- Attempt 1: move the registry of keys from `parse_cache.rs` into `parse_ahead.rs`: 62,145,865 (no change). Attempt 2: replace the `Mutex<Vec>` by a table of 1024 `AtomicU64` tags (no `Vec` and no `Mutex` instances): 62,146,235 (no change). Both were reverted. The 2 attempts are used up: stopped as the rule says.
- The cost is a +1 instruction in the hot dispatch of the regexp matcher, set by a partition of the codegen units that no source change controls. Any change in `bare-js` can move it in either direction. A hypothesis for a lasting fix (not built): a matcher loop that does not need the table address in a register (fewer live values in `run`), and a design document first (CLAUDE.md, "How to improve a part").

**Not tested.** Gmail settle, peak RSS and the first-byte mode of the 12 Gmail runs. A second pass of the matrix on a quiet machine. A build with `-C relocation-model=static` (it would remove the table base, but it is a change for the whole project).

### Proportional text (#603, 2026-11-16)

- Done: `font-family` is an inherited property with two values, `monospace` and `sans-serif` (the first entry of the list decides). The `font` shorthand sets it. The browser style sheet makes `pre`, `code`, `kbd`, `samp`, `tt`, `listing`, `plaintext` and `xmp` monospace. Layout measures a letter with the advance of its face. Paint draws with the same face, and takes the Noto Sans Mono glyph for the arrows, math signs and shapes that Noto Sans lacks.
- Tests: new tests in `bare-css` (family, inheritance, `font`, the UA rule), `bare-layout` (`font::tests`: Noto Sans advances, `monospace` keeps 0.6 em, the first entry decides, bold), and `bare-paint` (the advance tables against the font files, Sans glyph pen positions against layout widths). The older tests keep their numbers: their pages set `html { font-family: monospace }` (a helper of each test file), because their expected sizes come from a letter of 0.6 em. Their boxes would otherwise have no wrap where the test expects one.
- Found by a test: a box has no fragment of its own when its `Metrics` equal those of its parent. `Metrics` now holds the face, so it compares only size, ascent and descent. Without that, a `<b>` inside a span got its own fragments, and `getClientRects` of the span changed.
- Memory: `ComputedStyle` is 880 bytes, 8 more than before (one slot for `font-family`).
- Picture: a Hacker News-like table (`Verdana, Geneva, sans-serif`, 10pt), old build `/tmp/hn-old.png`, new build `/tmp/hn-new.png`. The second title fits on one line in the new picture, and wraps in the old one. `<code>` stays monospace.
- Not measured: layout and paint time and instruction counts with the tables (`width_of` does a binary search for a letter outside ASCII). Not compared with Chrome: no page was laid out in Chrome with Noto Sans. Gaps: `getComputedStyle().fontFamily` gives the face, not the list (#516, #587); `<input>` and `<button>` still take the family of their parent, and the default width of a text control still uses 0.644 em per `size` unit (`controls.rs`); `serif` text is Noto Sans.
## `shot` waits for the page scripts (2026-11-16)

`shot` waited for the document and the pictures only. It could take the picture before a page script ran or before the requests of a script ended. Now `shot` waits by the rule of `ready`: the document is in, `load` ran, `Page::idle` is `Ok` on two looks in a row, and no picture loads. This holds in step files and in the MCP `screenshot` tool. The wait ends at the step time limit. The picture is then taken anyway, and the step note says `not ready: ...`. Tests: `crates/drive/tests/shot_ready.rs`. Not tested: a live page such as `https://example.com/`.

`Page::paint_at` called `build_band` and `draw_view` directly, so a windowed journey had no `paint` records. Now `DisplayList::make` writes `paint/build` and `Painter::draw_view` writes `paint/draw`. `paint/paint` stays as the outer span of the headless `Painter::paint`. Both new spans are lazy: with tracing off they do no work. Test: `paint_trace_tests` in `crates/bare` runs two window paints of a page with an input. It finds one `build` and two `draw` records with the session id, and no file with `BARE_OBSERVE=off`. The parent reran the windowed journey once in an isolated Cage screen. It passed with 406 records, 4 `paint/build`, 19 `paint/draw`, a `session_id` on each paint record and zero drops. Not tested: the cost of the spans with tracing on, and non-Linux.

## HTTP/2 first-frame trace record (2026-11-17)

Added `network/h2_ttfb` (field `duration_ns`): the wait from the end of the request writes to the first frame of the reply on the reader thread. With tracing off, a stream stores `None` and the request path takes no `Instant::now()`, no allocation and no new lock. The reader adds one branch per frame. The new test `h2_ttfb_is_the_wait_for_the_first_frame` (a 150 ms server wait, a child process with `BARE_OBSERVE=trace`) failed before the change (no record) and passes after it. The h2 suites keep their counts: 28, 8, 4, 14 and 30 passed. Not tested: error-before-headers outcomes, a release build, a tracing-on CPU cost. Detail: `docs/monitoring.md`.

## Pre-header request failure record (2026-11-17)

Added `network/request_failed` (fields `kind`, `retried`, `replay`, `duration_ns`): one record when a request fails before its response headers. `kind` is a code for the `cause::describe` kind. The record has no URL, host or error text. The success path adds one gated `Instant::now()` at entry to `start()` (trace mode only; with monitoring off it is one atomic load). The new test `a_request_that_fails_before_its_headers_has_a_record` (refused connect, a server that closes with no reply, one good request; a child process with `BARE_OBSERVE=trace`, `metrics` and `off`) failed before the change (0 records) and passes after it. `bare-net` lib keeps 173 passed, 1 ignored; `h2_observe` 12, `h2_edge` 28 and driver `monitoring` 4 pass. Not tested: TLS, DNS, HTTP/2 and replay failures end to end, a release build, a tracing-on CPU cost. Detail: `docs/monitoring.md`.

## Logger queued memory (2026-11-17)

`bare-observe` now counts the heap bytes of records that wait in its queue (`Vec::capacity`): current, peak, and peak record count. Each process sample has `logger_queued_bytes`. The terminal `collector_status` record has `peak_queued_bytes` and `peak_queued_records`. `Status` and `Handle::queued_bytes()` expose them. The producer adds a few relaxed atomic operations per queued record. With monitoring off, no collector exists, so none run. The worst-case terminal record is 319 bytes, within the 512-byte reserve. The new test `queued_memory_is_counted_and_released` failed to compile before the change and passes after it. `bare-observe` has 13 unit tests (was 12) and 4 process tests; `bare-os` 10; the doctest 1. Driver `monitoring` 4 and MCP `monitoring` 1 pass. `cargo check --workspace` passes. Not counted: producer-local record buffers, the channel slot array, and the writer's OS and file buffers. Not tested: a release build, a tracing-on CPU cost of the counters, a capture that subtracts the counter from RSS, Windows and macOS runs.
## `sessions` names a session with no document, and the hidden iframe download test (#573, #585, 2026-11-16)

- #573: after a `goto` that fails, `sessions` printed `main: `. Now it prints `main: (no document: the document did not load: network error: connect refused)`. A session with no document and no error prints `main: (no document)`. `load_document` now keeps the kind of the cause (`dns`, `connect refused`, `read timeout`, `reset`...) from `bare_net::cause::describe`. It drops the error text, because the text can name a host or a URL. New test: `sessions_names_a_session_whose_document_did_not_load` (failed before, passes after).
- #585: root cause is the test, not the product. The wait loop counted `" bytes"` in the list. A running download prints `running: <url> (0 bytes)`, so the loop ended at once (the test ended in 0.03 s) and the check for `report.csv (` ran before the file was saved. The loop now counts `" bytes, "`, which only a finished download prints. Before: 5 failures in 10 runs. After: 0 in 10.

- `getComputedStyle(el).font` threw `Unsupported`. It now gives the Chrome text: style, weight, size, `/ line-height` and family, and it leaves out a `normal` style, a 400 weight and a `normal` line height (for example `italic 700 20px / 30px monospace`, `16px sans-serif`).
- `getComputedStyle(el).transform` and `webkitTransform` were `undefined`, because `transform` is not in the property list of the style block. The computed object now has its own read-only accessors. The value is `none`, or `matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, tx, ty)` for a translate in px. Left: the engine keeps only the move, so rotate and scale read as `none`, `translate(0, 0)` reads as `none` (Chrome gives a matrix), and a percent move is gated (it needs the box). `el.style.transform` is still not supported. #558 is `Refs`, not closed.
- `innerText` over a `select` threw. Now each `option` of the select (also in an `optgroup`) is one line, as in Chrome. Options have `display: none` in the UA sheet, so the walk reads them from the select. A hidden select gives nothing.

## Legacy mouse event members (#568, 2026-11-16)

Gmail code reads old members of mouse events. Now `MouseEvent` has `which`, `sourceCapabilities`, `layerX`, `layerY`, `fromElement`, `toElement` and `initMouseEvent` (15 arguments, no effect while the event dispatches). `KeyboardEvent` and `InputEvent` have `which` and `sourceCapabilities`. The code is in `browser_mouse_legacy.rs`. Each getter computes its value when read. An event stores nothing new.

- `which` of a mouse event is `button + 1` for `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `click`, `dblclick`, `auxclick` and `contextmenu`, and 0 for other types.
- Approximations: `sourceCapabilities` is always `null` (no `InputDeviceCapabilities`). `layerX` and `layerY` count from the border box of the nearest positioned ancestor, not from the nearest paint layer. bare has no `UIEvent` interface, so the members sit on the three interfaces.
- Tests: `browser_mouse_legacy_tests.rs`, 9 tests. Not compared with Chrome. Not tested: Gmail. This change alone may not fix #568.

## Load-flaky tests, round 2 (2026-11-17)

- Product bug: `Dom::layout_shared` keyed its cached layout by the address of the `Styles`. A freed address could come back for new styles, so a read used the layout of the old ones. Now the cascade drops the cached layout when it builds new `Styles` (one `RefCell` take for each full cascade, nothing for a read). Test: `a_new_sheet_is_never_read_with_the_layout_of_the_old_one`. Without the fix it fails 10/10 (round 5). Cause of the flake in `external_sheets_embedded_sheets_and_inline_styles_cascade_in_order`: hypothesis, not reproduced alone. A `Weak<Styles>` in the cache was tried first. It makes `Rc::get_mut` fail, so in-place restyle stops: 6 tests in `browser_computed*_tests` failed. Not used.
- Loader parallel tests (`browser_loader/parallel_tests.rs`): no wall-clock bound any more. The server holds a request until 3 are inside together, so a loader that sends them one at a time fails at the deadline and a correct one passes at any speed.
- `a_refused_range_goes_back_to_the_first_connection`: the job fails when the first connection ends before a refused range is given back to it. The test throttled that connection to 16 MiB/s, so it relied on timing. Verified: with no throttle it fails 20/20 on an idle machine. The server now holds the first body until the test sees that every split segment is refused and given back. No product change: that failure is correct for a real server. I did not reproduce the old flake (10 runs with 16 and 64 `yes` loads, 6 runs of the module).
## @property initial-value (2026-11-16, issue #586)
## @property initial-value (2026-11-17, issue #586, redesign)

`@property` is now a registry in the `RuleSet` (`registered`: name, initial value, inherits). It adds no rule. The first version (PR #588) added a `*` rule for each `inherits: false` property, and a `*` rule is matched against every element on every restyle.

Design: `var::Sets` reads the registry when it looks up a custom property. An element does not take a registered `inherits: false` value from its parent; the lookup gives the initial value. `var(--x)` of a registered property with no value gives the initial value. An element that has no custom property of its own shares the set of its parent only when that set holds no `inherits: false` value (`Sets::blocks_sharing`, O(1)). `@property` inside `@layer` and `@media` is read. `CSS.registerProperty` adds an `@property` text as the last sheet part and restyles; a second call with the same name is `InvalidModificationError`, a bad name or syntax is `SyntaxError`.

Numbers (`cascade_load file`, 2,003 elements, 40 `@property` rules with `inherits: false`, `compute` x 20, `instructions:u`, 3 runs): PR #588 version (75cd58f7) 332,256,467 / 332,256,596 / 332,256,700. Registry 87,710,238 / 87,721,426 / 87,736,839. That is 3.8 times fewer. Same check sum. The result with no `@property` rule is not changed.

Tests: `registered_property_in_layer_and_media_and_perf` (also: 50 `@property` rules add 0 rules), `register_property_from_code`, `register_property_gives_the_initial_value_and_restyles`. The first one fails on 75cd58f7 (checked with its assertions, without `is_registered`).

Not tested: the page of the issue in `bare-mcp`. Syntax types are not checked. A name that a style sheet `@property` has is not a duplicate for `registerProperty`.

Seen, not fixed: `browser_geometry_tests::external_sheets_embedded_sheets_and_inline_styles_cascade_in_order` fails with this change. The layout cache (`browser_scroll.rs:384`) keys on `Rc::as_ptr(styles)`, and a bigger `RuleSet` makes the allocator reuse the address of the old rules (hypothesis, from the key and the stale 77x30; not proven with a tool). A parallel agent owns the layout cache.
## `computed-nodes` stopped a long SPA session (#550, 2026-11-16)

- Cause: the node arena is freed only by a collect and a reclaim. The page driver collected when the script heap grew (`Interp::gc_due`). A page that replaces a list makes many dead nodes and almost no script heap, so no collect ran. The arena grew with every replace. `computed-nodes` counted `Document::len` (all slots, with free ones), so it fired while the live tree was small.
- Fix: `Browser::collect_due` also asks for a collect when the arena has grown by 2 MiB (or a fourth of the live bytes) since the last one; the page driver and `ui_call` use it. `computed-nodes` counts `live_len`, as the DOM cap already did. The cap is not changed.
- Test: `replacing_a_list_many_times_does_not_reach_computed_nodes` (700 rows of 5 nodes, replaced 50 times, one `getComputedStyle` after each). Before: `computed-nodes` at round 37, `len` 133,006. After: `len` stays at 108,506 from round 32 to round 49.
- Not tested: live Gmail; the `goto` case of the issue (a new document should have a small arena; not reproduced); peak RSS (arena slots peak at 108,506; without the fix they grow by 3,500 a round, so 175,006 at round 50 by calculation, one run).
## Computed `transform` as a matrix (#558, 2026-11-17)

`getComputedStyle(el).transform` gave `none` for rotate, scale, skew and `matrix()`, `none` for `translate(0, 0)`, and threw for a percent move. Vaul parses this value in `getTranslate`. Now any list that is not `none` reads as `matrix(a, b, c, d, e, f)` in Chrome's number format (`1.23457e+06`, `1e-05`). A percent is of the border box, read with a layout only when the list has a percent.

- Memory: a plain move (units agree, not zero) stays in `TranslateX` and `TranslateY` as before. Any other list is a `Grid::Transform` in the shared grid table, and `TranslateX` holds its index. The style of an element grows by 0 bytes. A list is stored once per page. The list keeps the steps (translate, or one folded matrix), not one matrix, because a percent after a rotation mixes the width and the height into the move.
- Layout moves a box by the move of the matrix. Paint still does not rotate or scale. This is out of scope.
- A real 3D step (`rotateX`, `rotateY`, `perspective`, a z move that is not 0, a `matrix3d` that is not flat) is a good value. It moves nothing, and the read is gated, because Chrome writes `matrix3d(...)`.
- Chrome (headless, this machine) writes `matrix(0, 1, -1, 0, 0, 0)` for `rotate(90deg)`, not `6.12323e-17`. A multiple of 90 degrees is exact here too. Expected values in the tests come from that Chrome.
- Changed on purpose: a mix of units (`translateX(5px) translateX(7%)`) is now a good value, as in Chrome. `calc()` inside a list that needs a matrix is still dropped.
- Not done: the `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` properties do not join the matrix. Not tested: Vaul itself, a transition of a matrix.
## 2026-11-17: Backspace and Delete merge blocks (#443)

Backspace at the start of a block with content moves its children to the end of the block before it. Delete at the end of a block moves the next block into it. The code is `delete_at_block_edge` in `browser_editing.rs`, ported, simplified, from the W3C editing draft "delete" command ("merge blocks") and Ladybird `command_delete_action` (BSD-2).

- A list before the block gives its last item; a next list gives its first item. The first item of a list leaves the list, as for an empty item (#499). Inline formatting moves with the children.
- Gaps: only sibling blocks merge. The last item of a list does not take the block after the list. A block nested in a `div` is not merged with a block outside it.
- Tests: 3 new in `browser_editing_tests.rs`. Not compared with Chrome in a live browser.
## Shift+Arrow extends the selection (#444, 2026-11-16)

Shift with ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Home and End now extends the selection in a `contenteditable` host. Control makes it by word, or to the end of the host with Home and End. `Selection.modify("move" | "extend", direction, granularity)` is built (granularities `character`, `word`, `lineboundary`, `paragraphboundary`, `documentboundary`). It reads the text of the host once per call, and cuts lines at blocks and `<br>`. In `<input>` and `<textarea>`, Control+Shift+Arrow now moves the selection end by word (`word_move`, shared with `modify`). No new crate: the word rule is the one of `word_at`. Tests: `browser_editing_tests` (three new tests). Before the change they failed ("" instead of "ld"; `modify` was a gate).

Not done: a double click or triple click on text in a `contenteditable` or plain text. A press has no hit test from a point to a text offset outside text fields (`caret_in` in `page.rs` reads the field layout only). Input and textarea already select a word and a line. Not tested: a real pointer on a laid-out page, Chrome comparison of word boundaries with punctuation, plain arrows (no Shift) in a host.

## Double and triple click select text (#444 part 2, 2026-11-16)

A double click on text in a `contenteditable` host or in plain page text now selects the word under the pointer. A triple click selects the nearest block (a paragraph, list item, heading, table cell or the host). Before, the selection stayed collapsed. Input and textarea are unchanged. New: a hit test from a window point to a Text node and a UTF-16 offset (`browser_rects::text_at`), and `document.caretRangeFromPoint(x, y)`.

How the hit test works: `bare_paint::hit` names the top element at the point. The box of that element (or of the nearest ancestor that has one) gives a range of fragments. The Text fragments in that range, whose node is inside the top element, are scored by distance to the point (line first, then side). The nearest wins. The letter boundary nearest to `x` comes from one walk over the letters of that fragment, with the advances and spacing of `Pass::x_at`. No layout runs again. Cost: one hit test (one pass over the fragments), one scan for the box, then the fragments of that box and the letters of one fragment.

Tests: three new tests in `browser_editing_tests`. Before the change, all three failed. After, they pass.

Not done or not tested: `caretPositionFromPoint` (no `CaretPosition` interface yet). A word is cut at the Text node (`he<b>llo</b>` selects one part). A triple click in a block that holds a nested block selects the nested text too. A single press on plain text does not move the caret (a press in a host still puts it at the end). Not tested: scrolled containers, `position: fixed` and sticky text, right-to-left text, a comparison with Chrome on a real page.

## Calls of other scripts and natives stay in the loop (`call-lane`, 2026-11-17)

Steps 1 and 2 of `docs/design-lane-calls.md`. Base: origin/main `632de066ae` (PR #636). Machine: archMachine. `Auto`, public React page, `#a1`. Instruction counts: minimum of 3 `perf stat` runs, spread at most 0.05%. Narrow rows: `byte`, scale 10.

- `Compiled` records its script. `CallR` runs a lane function of any script in the loop of the caller: no `select`, no `bc_call` chain, no nested `bc_loop`. Ops that read the tables of the current script call `bc_sync` first, outside the hot arms. A callee with an environment is set up in a cold function (`bc_call_env`). The unit tests run in a poison mode (feature `bc-poison` outside the tests): `select` parks an empty `prog` and `cc`, so a missing `bc_sync` panics. The mode caught a sync that was removed on purpose.
- A native callee gets the register slice of the caller as its arguments (`bc_call_r`): no argument copy, no `call_fn_inner`. `bcstats` has a new counter `natives`.
- The register stack grows by half of its size, not by the doubling of `Vec`. Calls of other scripts now share one deep stack, and the doubling kept up to twice its depth: +87,004 B of peak heap at 5 keys (massif). With the change the difference is +49,644 B.

| Row | main | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page load | 472.11M | 441.03M (-6.6%) |

## Profile of the lane after the calls work (`docs/research-lane-profile-after-calls.md`, 2026-11-17)

Base: origin/main `4d4b5e5442`. Machine: archMachine. `Auto`, public React page, `#a1`. No engine change. Callgrind groups are by name pattern, so approximate.

| Group | Load | Steady 5 keys (712.6M) | Steady 50 keys (6730.6M) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bytecode loop | 22.4% | 45.4% | 47.7% |
| Call setup | 2.2% | 3.0% | 3.1% |
| Property slow paths | 17.9% | 27.4% | 28.8% |
| GC | 0.1% | 5.8% | 4.9% |
| Parse and compile | 29.3% | 0.6% | 0.1% |
| Builtins | 3.3% | 1.4% | 1.0% |
| `select` | 0.2% | 0.2% | 0.2% |
| Other | 24.5% | 14.7% | 14.2% |

- Call setup fell from 16.4% to 3.0% of the steady page and `select` from 2.0% to 0.2%: calls are no longer a lever.
- Op histogram at 50 keys: 54.5M ops (59.5M before), 22 ops cover 90%. The best 8 fused pairs remove 16.2% of dispatches, the best 32 remove 25.1%. A dispatch costs 11.0 to 25.7 instructions.
- Narrow JIT upper bound (hypothesis): 5.5% to 12.9% of the page at 50 keys and 2.5% to 5.7% at load, before its own compile cost. It cannot touch the property slow paths (28%), GC, out-of-line operators (6.8%), malloc, natives or parsing (29% of load).
- Ranked levers (share of the 50-key run): (1) `to_uint32` fast path: every `BitAnd` and `BitOr` calls `trunc` and `fmod` (about 2M `fmod` calls at 50 keys); a 4-line throwaway change gave 50 keys 7167.75M to 7044.42M (-1.72%) and load 441.23M to 437.58M (-0.83%); (2) for-in key cache: `for_in_keys` is 4.0%, about 4,150 instructions per loop entry; (3) B1 `NewLit`: `DefField` is 4.3%; (4) copy by shape: `Object.assign` 2.4% and spread/rest 1.7%; (5) keyed `GetElem` and `SetElem` caches: 6.8% (key mix not measured); (6) `GetField` slow path 3.1% (real miss rate 3.7%); (7) fewer GC collections: 5.2%, raises peak memory; (8) fused pairs 1.4% to 3.2%; (9) narrow JIT. The call-site cache is worth 0.5% to 0.7% and a cheaper `select` under 0.2%.
- Decision: levers 1 to 5 remove a kind of work and together come to about 10% to 13%, close to the whole JIT bound, at lower risk. Build the `to_uint32` fast path first; design for-in key cache, `NewLit` and copy by shape before building. The narrow JIT design doc waits.
- Not tested: unit tests, clippy, `exec_diff.sh`, cost matrix, narrow rows and peak memory for the `to_uint32` experiment; the `GetElem` and `SetElem` key mix; how polymorphic the `GetField` misses are; the same-shape share of `Object.assign` and spread.

## For-in key design and keyed access research (`docs/design-for-in-keys.md`, `docs/research-keyed-access.md`, 2026-11-17)

Base: origin/main `4d4b5e5442`. `Auto`, public React page, `#a1`, callgrind with a symbols build. No engine code kept.

- For-in: `for_in_keys` is 304.5M of 7,177.9M (4.24%) at 50 keys: 4,206 instructions for each of 72,406 loop entries (`own_keys` copies 81.4M, seen-set inserts 71.4M, `peek_own_property` 71.2M, `Vec` growth 30.8M). All 72,406 entries are plain shape-mode objects with prototype `Object.prototype`; loops average 5.03 keys over 147 shapes. Recommended design B: read keys in place from the shape table and skip `has_property` while the receiver keeps its shape. A throwaway prototype (reverted): load 441.29M to 433.92M (-1.67%), 5 keys 1152.39M to 1111.83M (-3.52%), 50 keys 7167.78M to 6823.40M (-4.80%); output, render counts and `bcstats` equal; RSS no growth (medians of 7 fresh-copy runs). Safety condition: no shape sweep while a loop is open (`collect` refuses at `depth != 0` today). Not run on the prototype: full tests, clippy, `exec_diff.sh`, narrow rows, cost matrix. Waits for the owner's review.
- Keyed access: `GetElem` and `SetElem` ops are 517.5M, 7.7% of the steady page (648,770 `GetElem` at 387 instructions; 263,492 `SetElem`). Two classes make 77% of the cost, both a short string key on a plain object: `SetElem` that adds a key (196,075 ops at 1,064 each, 3.10%; three lookups of the same key) and `GetElem` of an own property (474,375 ops at 405 each, 2.85%). Array index keys are about 1.2%. Sources: a few for-in loops of the bundle (the JSX props copy, rest-props copies, DOM prop diff); the top 10 sites run 69.5% of the keyed ops. A per-site cache does not fit (the key changes on every pass; one entry hits 5.8%, four entries 18.0%). Ranked (hypothesis): (1) a global (shape, key) cache in out-of-line functions, 3.5% to 5.5% of the steady page; (2) the for-in design extended with slot indices; (3) array dense read, write and append fast paths, about 1%; (4) one-character string table, about 0.1%.
- Not tested: any keyed fast path (no code built); the hit rate of a global (shape, key) table; the private dashboard journey.

## For-in reads keys in place from the shape table (`forin-keys-in-place`, 2026-11-17)

Design: `docs/design-for-in-keys.md`, designs B and C. `for_in_keys` was 4.24% of the 50-key page (4,206 instructions for each of 72,406 loop entries): it copied the own keys, built a seen set and a `Vec`, and called `has_property` at each step. Now a loop over a shape-mode object reads the keys in place from the shape table and skips `has_property` while the receiver keeps its shape. A receiver that is not a proxy and has no prototype keys skips the seen set (an exotic receiver too: its own keys are unique); a proxy keeps it, because its `ownKeys` trap may repeat a key. A loop opened outside a call or statement frame takes the list path: the lane also runs script bodies at `depth == 0`, where `collect` can run, so the doc's `depth >= 1` assertion would fire on correct code. Base: origin/main `37618a88`. Machine: archMachine. `Auto`, public React page, `#a1`; minimum of 3 runs, spread at most 0.005%. Narrow rows: `byte`, scale 10.

| Row | main | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page load | 436.88M | 429.38M (-1.72%) |
| Page 50 keys | 7020.61M | 6674.56M (-4.93%) |
| loopfn / fib / calls / loop / closures | 837.06 / 58.21 / 1599.28 / 2369.05 / 466.69M | 831.05 / 58.25 / 1603.28 / 2373.05 / 467.29M (-0.72% / +0.07% / +0.25% / +0.17% / +0.13%) |

- Cost matrix against main (803 rows): 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators. `wrapper_load forin` 1000 rows -3.33% glibc / -2.32% jemalloc, 10000 rows -4.86% / -4.45%; `arrobj_load descriptors` 1 -0.82% / -0.44%, 10 -1.38% / -1.23%; `eval_load objects` 1 -0.14% / -0.13%, 10 +0.007% / +0.013% (its for-in work fell from 494K to 169K instructions; +139K comes from `bc_loop` itself, a layout shift of two edited arms). A first step-2 version made `wrapper_load forin` +1.6% / +2.3% because `for_in_step` was no longer inlined; skipping the seen set for exotic receivers fixed it.

- Tests: `cargo test -p bare-js --lib` 1024 passed, 1 ignored. 25 new loop cases and the 33 existing ones run in Tree, Auto and Byte against Node 22 values; counter tests `for_in_shape` and `for_in_sets` failed first; a `collect` that sweeps shapes between two loops keeps the keys; a 100,000-key dictionary object still hits the step limit. `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences. test262 for-in subset: pass 108, fail 19, the same in `tree`, `auto` and `byte`.

## Keyed table for `GetElem` and `SetElem` (`keyed-cache`, 2026-11-17)

Design: `docs/design-keyed-cache.md`, design A with a compact table. `GetElem` of an own string key and `SetElem` that adds a key were 77% of the keyed cost (7.7% of the steady page); a per-site cache cannot serve them because the key changes on every pass of a for-in loop. Now `Heap` holds one 2-way table of 2,048 entries of 32 bytes (64 KiB) keyed by (shape, key atom). It reuses `ic_hit`, `ic_store`, `ic_add`, `ic_fill` and `set_fill`. The fast path is out of line, at the top of `bc_get_elem` and in a new `bc_set_elem` (called for string keys only). A shape sweep empties the table. A write entry is filled at the second miss of its pair, so unique-key adds (`o['k'+i] = i`) do not pay a fill on every write. Base: origin/main `75c2b1e3`. Machine: archMachine. `Auto`, public React page, `#a1`; minimum of 3 runs, spread at most 0.012%. Narrow rows: `byte`, scale 10.

| Row | main | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page load | 429.18M | 425.01M (-0.97%) |
| Page 50 keys | 6674.50M | 6440.38M (-3.51%) |
| loopfn / fib / calls / loop | 831.05 / 58.25 / 1603.28 / 2373.05M | 831.07 / 58.26 / 1603.29 / 2373.06M (at most +0.02%) |
| closures | 467.29M | 467.75M (+0.10%) |
| Peak RSS load / 50 keys (byte copies, medians of 7) | 26936 / 35276 KiB | 26596 / 35140 KiB (-1.3% / -0.4%) |

- Cost matrix against main (803 rows): 0 rows over +0.5% under either allocator. The first version had 5 rows over (`arrobj_load objects` up to +1.5%, `descriptors`, `adapter_load u8steps 10`, `promise_load fanout 10`): unique-key adds paid a fill on every write, and numeric-key `SetElem` paid an extra out-of-line call. Both are fixed.
- `bcstats`, render counts and steps per key (82,227) are unchanged.
- Tests: `cargo test -p bare-js --lib` 1028 passed, 1 ignored. 19 cases from the design's test list run in Tree, Auto and Byte against Node 22 literals; 3 more check that the lane hits the table (Tree gets 0 hits), that a shape sweep empties it, and that two realms keep their own entries. Removing the sweep reset fails the sweep test; ignoring the prototype epoch fails the comparison with Node through the debug `ic_verify` check. Ignoring the key's generation number is not caught (no test frees an atom and reuses its slot). `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences.
- One difference from Node that also exists on main: `undefined[k] = 1` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined" where Node says "Cannot set properties". All three modes agree; the test compares the error name only.
- Step 2 of the design (single-search `Heap::set`) is not built. After the table, most adds on the page never reach `Heap::set`; the estimate is about -0.8% at 50 keys, below the gate of -1%. This is an estimate from the design's call counts, not a measurement.
- Not tested: test262 (its runner ignores `BARE_JS_EXEC` and the default executor is Tree, so the new path does not run there); a callgrind split; the hit rate of the table on the page; a test that frees an atom and reuses its slot; wall time; Windows; the private dashboard journey; release builds of the deliberately broken versions.

One full run before that showed `downloads::run::tests::a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero` failing. It passed alone 3 of 3 and in the next full run (the same case failed in a full run on an earlier base, see the 3b entry).
- Cost gate (arjun-e16, `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh -j 6`, instruction counts): 803 rows in 53 s. Mean change: glibc +0.006%, jemalloc +0.000%. Over under one allocator: 0. Over under both: 0. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` fail to run (the known failure, base too). No codegen-units=1 check was needed.
- Known limits: a queued message that holds ports is dropped when its port moves (one console warning). After `close()` the wires that wait for the closed end are dropped. A message over the bounds of the receiver is dropped with a console warning.
- Not tested: the cost of a page that moves ports (no benchmark row has an iframe with a src), peak memory, wall time, live Gmail (the account menu), the real-time clock and live window mode with ports, GC with a split port across a `collect`, the bounds of the hub (`messages`, `message-bytes`), a port in a message that is dropped for an origin mismatch, a page that navigates while a port is in flight, `workers` (step 5).

## Chrome vs Bare on a live staging E2E: create and delete a client and an agent (2026-11-18)

Question: what does one real E2E test cost in Chrome over CDP and in Bare? The earlier comparison (resources.md, 2026-11-17) used a small local page. This one uses the live staging app.

Journey (one step file for both browsers): log in, create a client, create an agent with the 3-step wizard (setup, name and voice, review), delete the agent from its detail page, delete the client from its settings. A Node CDP driver runs the same step file in Chrome. It uses real mouse events and waits for a stable box before each click, as Playwright does. An API cleanup after each run found no leftover client.

Setup: archMachine, Bare `532cc4e9` (release `bare-drive`), Chrome 155.0.8059.39. Method as in resources.md: one systemd scope per browser, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, cgroup `cpu.stat` and `memory.peak`, a PSS sampler every 20 ms. Windowed runs ran in an isolated headless `cage`. Other agent threads, 29 containers, the Windows VM, 34 user timers and syncthing were paused. Load average stayed between 0.3 and 0.9. Runs alternated, with no warm-up, because trial runs had already warmed the caches: 6 headless pairs and 4 windowed pairs. All 20 runs passed. Values are means, with the spread as (max-min)/mean.

| metric | headless Chrome | headless Bare | ratio | windowed Chrome | windowed Bare | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| journey ms | 8,265 (14%) | 6,632 (13%) | 1.25x | 7,962 (10%) | 6,836 (7%) | 1.16x |
| CPU ms total | 5,117 (3%) | 3,948 (2%) | 1.30x | 5,510 (4%) | 4,453 (2%) | 1.24x |
| CPU ms user | 4,229 | 3,852 | 1.10x | 4,302 | 4,357 | 0.99x |
| CPU ms sys | 888 | 96 | 9.3x | 1,208 | 96 | 12.6x |
| instructions:u (M) | 25,403 (2%) | 29,652 (2%) | 0.86x | 28,032 (5%) | 34,458 (3%) | 0.81x |
| peak PSS MiB | 429 (3%) | 84 (2%) | 5.1x | 528 (1%) | 91 (5%) | 5.8x |
| peak RSS sum MiB | 1,217 | 87 | 14.1x | 1,403 | 94 | 14.9x |
| memory.peak MiB | 353 | 79 | 4.5x | 398 | 86 | 4.6x |
| processes | 13 | 1 | | 15 | 1 | |

The Chrome CDP driver is a separate process and is not in the Chrome columns: 280 ms CPU and 76 MiB RSS per run.

Findings:
- Memory is the clear gain: 5x less PSS and 14x less RSS. Bare runs as one process.
- On this app Bare runs about 17% to 23% more user instructions than Chrome, because the JS engine is a tree walker and V8 compiles. On the small page of resources.md Bare ran 250x fewer. The difference is the JS work of the page: here React and the staging app scripts are most of it. Hypothesis: the JIT and the lane work are what close this gap.
- Total CPU is still 1.24x to 1.30x lower in Bare, because Chrome spends 9x to 13x more system time (process start, IPC, GPU process).
- The journey is 1.16x to 1.25x faster in Bare. Most of the time is network and server wait.

Not tested: arjun-e16; a real Hyprland window (only headless `cage`); more than 6 and 4 runs; a Chrome profile with a warm HTTP cache across runs (each run used a fresh profile, and Bare has no disk cache); Playwright itself (a plain CDP driver was used). The scripts and raw results are local, in the session scratchpad: `chrome_steps.mjs`, `harness.py`, `monitor.py`, `report.py`, `out-main/`.

## Where Bare spends CPU and memory on the staging E2E, and the bytecode lane on it (2026-11-18)

This entry splits the cost of the journey above (create and delete a client and an agent) by browser subsystem. It also measures the JS engine modes on the same journey. No product code changed.

- All 13 runs passed. The cleanup found no test client left.

| Part | MiB |
| --- | ---: |

| JS source and syntax trees (`with_shared_source` 9.7, `parse_cache` 2.1) | 12.9 |

## 2026-11-18: collector counters (plan step P0.2)

`BARE_JS_STATS=1` now prints one `gcstats` line per realm when the realm ends: collections, young objects (made since the last collect), young objects that survived their first collect, and `task_alloc_max` (the largest heap growth between two safe points, that is one task). These numbers size the young space and the in-task trigger of the hybrid collector (design section 10, Q11).

Cost (`tools/js/instr.sh`, `BARE_JS_EXEC=auto`, `eval_load`, base `d89f0299`): objects 10 +0.010%, closures 10 +0.026%, throws 10 +0.046% instructions.

Typing page (`type_load /data/bare-tmp/jit-page '#a1' 50`, `auto`, 3 runs, the same each time): 13 collections, 438,033 young objects, 96,567 kept (22.0%), `task_alloc_max` 4,388,944 B (4.19 MiB).

Staging journey (archMachine, `auto`, 3 runs, all `ok`, 4 realms each):

| Run | Collections | Young objects | Kept | Survival | Largest task |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 20 | 814,994 | 262,015 | 32.2% | 4,227,240 B |
| 2 | 21 | 838,012 | 270,910 | 32.3% | 4,227,240 B |
| 3 | 18 | 727,376 | 247,451 | 34.0% | 4,222,208 B |

- Between 22% and 34% of young objects survive their first collect. That is high for a young generation: V8 and others plan for about 10% or less. Hypothesis: one collect covers many tasks, so objects that live for a few tasks count as kept. A per-task count would split them.
- No task on these workloads grows the heap by more than 4.2 MiB. An in-task trigger at a few MiB would rarely fire here; it matters for loops like `eval_load throws`.

Not tested: per-task survival, other journeys, the e16 machine.
## Engine rewrite design: two rounds of a four-model review (2026-11-18)

- Design: `docs/design-engine-rewrite.md` (PR #681). Reviewers: Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol and GPT-6.2 Astra, high effort, one brief on data structures and algorithms for resource use. Static review; no builds or journeys ran.
- Round 1 added section 6.10 (23 changes). Round 2 added section 6.11 (19 changes) and corrected five items of round 1.
- Facts checked against the code: the collector copies every live binding and script string into one roots `Vec` (`eval.rs:932-941`); the object slab at the peak is a doubled `Vec` (one 13,631,488-byte block); constant operands exist only for numbers on the right side of a compare; `switch` is a linear chain; `gc_due` collects only between tasks; parse-ahead copies the text before its duplicate check; a DOM wrapper makes the wrappers of all ancestors.
- New measurement (1 run, `auto`): samples with a collector frame anywhere on the stack are 1,229 of 13,026 (9.4% of CPU). The leaf-first split showed 4.7%.
- Round 2 corrections: the write barrier may be skipped only when no collection can happen before the store; ropes stay; runtime atoms stay weak; cache records live in a per-realm feedback vector, not in shared code; the dictionary cache entry is kept, not lost.
- Open owner questions: section 10, items 2 to 4 and 6 to 13.

## Owner decision: the engine rewrite targets the daily workload (2026-11-18)

- Decision: the new engine is built and tuned for the daily journeys (the staging journey, the typing page and the public journeys). No speculating JIT. The baseline JIT is optional and is built only if a profile of the daily journeys shows hot code that pays for it. The interpreter is a full engine.
- A feature census of the daily journeys on today's engine (new in S0) decides which language features and built-ins are ported. A feature outside the census throws a `TypeError` that names it and is logged.
- Why: on short, cold code a JIT does not pay back its start cost (Node: about 94 M instructions and 46 MiB at start), and QuickJS without a JIT is 1.6 to 3.8 times below today's `auto` (`research-quickjs-reference.md`).
- Design: `docs/design-engine-rewrite.md` section 6.12 (PR #681).

## Engine rewrite: open design questions decided (2026-11-18)

- The owner asked for the best choice for speed and resource use on each open question of `docs/design-engine-rewrite.md` section 10. Each answer there lists the reasons for and against.
- Values: NaN-boxing; compressed slots only if the S1 census shows value slots are a large share of the peak.
- New crate next to the old one: yes.
- Collector: between tasks by default, and inside a task at the allocation slow path when the task passes the trigger, with compiler root maps (reason: `throws` 10 peaks at 32.4 MiB on Bare against 3.3 MiB on QuickJS).
- Disk code cache: allowed, cold against cold Chrome and warm against warm Chrome.
- Long sessions: memory must stay flat; a 20-round session row in S5; flushing and compaction only if it grows.
- Ready: the first journey step can act; the browser with all helpers counts; engine comparisons on a replayed network cache.
- Before S1: the measurements and two small compiler changes land in today's engine.
- Gates: S2 browser slice; `eval_load` at or below QuickJS on instructions in S2, and on peak RSS by S5.
- The speculating JIT is checked last (new stage S8), only if a daily-journey profile shows hot loops.

## 2026-11-18: effect context for `&&`, `||`, `?:` and comma (plan step P0.5)

An expression whose value nobody reads (`expr_void`) now compiles `a && b`, `a || b` and `c ? x : y` as a test and jumps. Each compare in the test is one fused op (`jump_cond`), and the parts that run keep no value either. In a comma expression, the parts before the last are `expr_void` too. Before, `a === 1 && f()` as a statement computed the compare into a register (`StrictEq`), then jumped on it (`JmpIfNot`). The golden listing `sequence` changes one temporary register; the op count is the same.

Staging journey with `bc-hist` (archMachine, `auto`, 2 runs each, all `ok`; base is main with the P0.3 counters):

| Build | Lane ops | Compare then `JmpIf`/`JmpIfNot` (top 40 pairs) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| base | 78.6 M, 79.3 M | 1.91%, 1.93% |
| P0.5 | 77.1 M, 76.5 M | 0.00%, 0.00% |

- Lane ops fall by about 2.8% (live pages: the spread between runs of one build is up to 1.8%).
- No compare and jump pair is left among the 40 most common pairs.

Cost rows (`tools/js/instr.sh`, `eval_load` at scale 10, `auto`, base main): every case within ±0.01%.

P0.4 (8.5%) and P0.5 (2.8%) together remove about 11% of the lane ops on the staging journey with two small changes to the code generator. This supports the design's view that the compiler can remove a large share of ops (design 6.11). Not measured: the two together, staging instructions without `bc-hist`, the typing page, Windows.

## 2026-11-18: constant operands on either side of a compare (plan step P0.4)

A fused compare and jump now takes a constant operand on either side. `1 < n` compiles as `n > 1` (`JnGtK`), and `null !== e` as `e !== null` (`JnSNeK`). The constant has no side effect, so the order of the operands does not matter. Equalities (`==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`) also take a string, `null` or `void 0` as the constant: the constant table gains `Const::Null` and `Const::Undefined`, and the verifier allows them and strings only on these four ops. `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` keep number constants only.

Staging journey with `bc-hist` (archMachine, `auto`, 2 runs each, all `ok`; base is main with the P0.3 counters):

| Build | Lane ops | `LoadI` | `LoadK` | `LoadNull` | `LoadUndef` | `Jn*K` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| base | 78.6 M, 79.3 M | 4.19%, 4.16% | 3.13%, 3.20% | 6.14%, 6.07% | 0.31%, 0.31% | 2.74%, 2.75% |
| P0.4 | 73.0 M, 71.7 M | 3.36%, 3.37% | 2.91%, 2.90% | 2.46%, 2.45% | 0.24%, 0.24% | 8.37%, 8.44% |

- Lane ops fall by about 8.5% (live pages: the spread between runs of one build is up to 1.8%).
- `LoadNull` falls from 6.1% to 2.5% of ops. Minified code writes `null!==e` and `void 0===t`.
- A first version that swapped only number constants moved `LoadI` from 4.2% to 3.3% and left `LoadNull` and `LoadK` as they were.

Cost rows (`tools/js/instr.sh`, `eval_load` at scale 10, `auto`, base main): every case within ±0.11% (`webpack` −0.11%). These programs seldom put a constant on the left.

Not tested: staging instructions and CPU without `bc-hist`, the typing page, Windows.

## 2026-11-18: NaN-boxed value (plan step S1.2)

`bare-js2` has a `Value` of 8 bytes (`crates/js2/src/value.rs`, design 6.1). A double is stored as it is. Every other value has a tag in the top 16 bits from `0xFFF9`: a 32-bit integer, `undefined`, `null` and the booleans, and pointers to a string, symbol, BigInt or object cell. "Is a double" is one unsigned compare. A NaN whose bits reach the tag space becomes the canonical NaN on entry (`Value::number`), with the same one compare. Pointers go through the exposed-provenance API, so the module has no `unsafe` code; the heap will hold the 48-bit address check (design 6.1); here it is a debug check.

Checks: 5 unit tests, also under Miri (nightly 2026-11-17), including a pointer round trip that reads the cell. Micro row `crates/js2/examples/value_load.rs` (archMachine, release, `tools/js/instr.sh`, min of 3): 327,816,398 instructions for 10,000,000 values and 315,465 for none, so 32.7 instructions per value for one encode and one decode of mixed kinds, with the loop and the checksum.

Not measured: the same row on today's 16-byte `Value`, arm64.

## 2026-11-18: size-class block allocator (plan step S1.3)

`bare-js2` has the allocator of its heap (`crates/js2/src/heap.rs`, design 6.10 item 15). A block is 64 KiB, aligned to its size, and comes from the new `bare_os::pages` module (`mmap` on Unix, `VirtualAlloc` on Windows, `std::alloc` under Miri). The block header holds the cell size and one mark bit per cell, so a mark finds its bit from the cell address with no table. A request of at most 8,192 bytes takes a cell of the smallest of 16 size classes. Each class has a free list through its free cells. A larger request gets a mapping of its own. Small blocks are swept lazily: a block is swept when its class next needs cells. A block with no live cell goes to a pool of 4 blocks; the rest go back to the OS. A block above the 48-bit address limit is given back, and the allocation fails.

Checks: 5 heap tests and 1 `pages` test, all 10 `bare-js2` tests also under Miri (nightly 2026-11-17). | heap | 211,217,586 | 21.1 | 12,016 to 12,344 KiB |

## 2026-11-18: host interface crate (plan step S0.2)

A new crate `crates/js-api` (`bare-js-api`) holds the interface between the browser and an engine. It has no engine code. The browser will be generic over its `Engine` trait, and a session picks the engine when it starts (owner decision, 2026-11-18). The host holds handles, not values: a `Local` (a slot in the handle stack of a `Scope`) or a `Persistent` (a slot in a table of the realm). A method that takes `&mut Scope` may collect; a method that takes `&Scope` never does. The decisions on the six questions of S0.1 are in `docs/design-host-interface.md`.

Checks: 4 unit tests with a toy engine (scope pops, escape of a value or an exception, persistent handles, arguments) and 5 doc tests. 4 of the doc tests must fail to compile, each with its error code: a local that leaves its scope (E0521), an inner local kept in the outer scope (E0521), a string borrow held across a call (E0502), and a released persistent handle (E0382). Clippy is clean. The 4 unit tests also pass on the Windows 11 VM (`cargo xwin test --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`).

Not done: no engine implements the trait yet (S0.3), so no instruction numbers.

## 2026-11-18: the old engine behind the host interface (plan step S0.3)

`bare-js` implements `bare_js_api::Engine` for `Interp` (`crates/js/src/eval_api.rs`). The handle stack and the persistent table are two vectors of `Value` in the realm. `Interp::roots` and `Interp::collect` treat both as roots. This engine collects only between tasks, so `safepoint` does nothing. A host set through the interface gets the host calls; the old `Host` path stays as it was and is checked first. An engine error that is not an exception crosses the interface as `Abort`. The original error waits in the realm, so a host that passes the abort on gives back the same error (a step limit stays `Limit(Steps)`).

Interface changes: `Engine` no longer needs `'static`, because `Interp` has a lifetime parameter. `Scope::engine` (hidden) lets an engine read a slot before the scope ends. `Host::call` takes `this` as `Local<'s>`.

Checks:

- 4 adapter tests with a host that is written only against the interface: host functions, a call back into script, a thrown value, an escape scope, a step limit through the host, a persistent handle through a collection, and plain values. The 42 old host tests pass.
- Windows: the adapter tests, the 10 `host_tests` and the `bare-js-api` tests pass on the Windows 11 VM (`cargo xwin test`, run on the VM).
- Cost rows (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, archMachine, base = the parent commit `cf3830c5`, 3 runs per row): no row over +0.5%; mean +0.004% (glibc). A first version that checked the interface host before the old host put 5 host-call rows over +0.5% (up to +0.91% on `select_load react 1000`). The interface path is now a cold function after the old host check.
- `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` abort (exit 134) on the base tree too, so they are not counted.

Not done: the browser does not use the interface yet (S0.4).

## 2026-11-18: timers in persistent handles (plan step S0.4, first PR)

Timers keep their callback and their arguments in persistent handles of `bare-js-api`, not in `Value`s that `sched_roots` reports. A cleared or finished timer drops its handles. The engine roots only live handles.

Interface changes:

- A `Persistent` frees its slot when it is dropped. It holds an `Rc` of the realm's `Slots`: one bit per slot of the persistent table. A drop clears the bit, so the slot is free at once and no root at the next collection. `Scope::release` is now the same as `drop`. `Engine::release` is replaced by `Engine::slots`.
- `persist` takes the lowest free slot. The roots of the table come from the bits, so a table that once held many handles costs one word per 64 slots at a collection.
- A timer argument that has no reference into the heap (undefined, null, a boolean, a number, a small BigInt) stays as it is. Only the other arguments get a handle.

Checks:

- Tests: a cleared, a finished and a waiting timer (only the waiting callback stays after a collection); the table does not grow over 3 rounds of 200 timers; object and string arguments survive a collection (this test fails when an object argument gets no handle). 41 scheduler tests, 4 adapter tests and 4 `bare-js-api` tests pass on Linux and on the Windows 11 VM.
- Cost matrix (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, archMachine, base = `9a2c5c5a`, 805 rows): 1 row over +0.5% under both allocators, `scheduler_load timers 10`, +0.780% glibc and +0.757% jemalloc. `mixed 1` and `mixed 10` are under +0.1%. `gen_load finally 10` is +0.501% under glibc only (jemalloc -0.002%). `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` abort on the base too.
- The cost of `timers 10` is real work, not codegen noise. With `-C codegen-units=1` on both trees: `timers 10` +0.64% glibc and +0.68% jemalloc; `timers 100` +0.70%. That is about 128 instructions per timer. One handle create and drop costs about 70 instructions, fully inlined (a loop of 1 M handles: 75 per handle). The rest is the timer call record and its drop.
- The owner grants a cost exception for `scheduler_load timers 10` (2026-11-18). Reason: design 6.8 names persistent handles for timers, and the old engine will be replaced.

Variants measured on `timers 10` (glibc, `instr.sh`):

| Variant | Change |
| --- | ---: |
| First version: a drop list, a free list, a handle for each argument | +2.76% |
| No `Rc` around the call record; no argument vector when there are no arguments | +1.58% |
| Free slots sorted and the table truncated at each collection | +2.90% (worse, not kept) |
| A live bitmap in the engine, with a drop list | +1.44% |
| The bitmap shared with the handles, no drop list (kept) | +1.36% |
| `#[inline]` on the handle functions (kept) | +1.30% |
| Primitive arguments without a handle (kept) | +0.77% |

Notes:

- `callgrind` counts of `scheduler_load` change by up to 1% between two runs of the same binary. Use `perf stat` (`instr.sh`) for A/B.
- `instr.sh` takes the case and the scale as two arguments. In zsh, `$r` with a space does not split; use `${=r}`.

Not done: the staging journey A/B. The other subsystems of S0.4.

## 2026-11-19: event listeners and event state through host owners (plan step S0.4, events)

Listeners and event state keep their engine values in `Traced` fields of `bare-js-api` (`docs/design-host-tracing.md`, option A). The owner of a value traces it. The old host `trace` no longer visits listeners and events.

Interface changes:

- `Traced<R>` holds a raw engine value. It is not a root, and it is not `Copy` or `Clone`. `Tracer::visit` visits one. `Tracer::visit_raw` is transitional: event paths use it for node wrappers until the wrapper step.
- `Engine` has `Raw`, `raw`, `raw_local`, `store_raw` (the write barrier point) and `set_host_owner`. `Host` has `trace(key, tracer)` and `prune(dead keys)`.
- The old engine keeps owners in a list of object and key pairs. `collect` reads the list when its work list is empty and traces the reached owners that it did not trace yet. The traced values also go to the heap roots, because the heap marks again from roots.

Browser changes:

- The owners are a target (its listener list) or an event object (`target`, `currentTarget`, `detail`, `relatedTarget`). The host key indexes an owner table. A freed key is reused.
- The key of a target is in its listener entry. An entry with a key stays when its list is empty, so a target that adds and removes listeners keeps one key. The entry goes when its target dies.
- A node without a wrapper is no owner. Its handler placeholder holds the global object until a wrapper exists.

Checks:

- New tests: a detached node whose listener holds the node is collected, and its key is reused; a live target with 300 add and remove rounds keeps one key (this check fails when an empty entry is removed); a window listener and an event kept by a script survive two collections; a chain of 50 owners, each reached only through the listener of the one before, survives. In `bare-js`, an owner keeps its value in the heap after 1000 new objects (this check fails when the traced values do not go to the heap roots).
- Linux: `bare` lib 1638 passed; `bare-js` lib 1045 passed; `bare-js-api` 5 passed and 1 doc test. Windows 11 VM: 336 event, handler, collect and listener tests of `bare`, 5 interface tests of `bare-js` and 5 tests of `bare-js-api` pass.
- Cost matrix (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh -j 4`, archMachine, base = origin/main `e3eb5b9b`, 3 runs per row, 805 rows): no row over +0.5% under both allocators. Mean change +0.017% (glibc). `form_load gates 1` and `gates 10` are +0.90% and +0.92% under glibc only (jemalloc -0.34% and -0.38%). `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` abort on the base too.

Versions measured (rows over +0.5% under both allocators):

| Version | Rows over |
| --- | ---: |
| An object to key map in the engine, probed for each marked object; a target to key map in the browser | 28 (`focus_load focus 10` +2.35%, `web_apis_load abort 10` +2.03%) |
| The owner list, read when the work list is empty | 2 (`abort 1` +0.94%, `abort 10` +1.04%) |
| The target key in the listener entry | 2 (`abort 1` +0.63%, `abort 10` +0.65%) |
| The key checked in place when a listener is added (kept) | 0 |

`callgrind` on `focus_load focus 1` showed where the first version spent: +627K instructions in the per-object probe, +286K in map inserts for each event, +249K in the map retain at each collection.

Not done: the staging journey A/B. The DOM wrappers (`by_node`) are the next step of S0.4; then `visit_raw` goes.

## 2026-11-19: node wrappers as owners (plan step S0.4, DOM wrappers)

Option A of `docs/design-dom-wrappers.md`. A node wrapper is the owner of its node target. Its host key is set when the wrapper is made.

Changes:

- `by_node` holds `Traced` values. `Host::trace(key)` for a node visits the wrappers of its parent, children, shadow host or root and template content, then the listeners of the node.
- `Host::prune(dead)` drops the `by_node` and `by_obj` entries and the listeners of a dead wrapper. The `Dom` branch of the old per-object hook and the `by_node` retain of the old prune are gone. `visit_raw` is gone.
- Engine: before marking, `collect` writes the host key of each owner into its mark table (`Seen`, the bits above 33). Marking an object returns the key, so an owner is traced as soon as it is marked. The first version scanned the owner list each time the work list was empty. That took one pass for each level of the tree.
- `IdTab::remove` no longer tests the page for emptiness (the test reads the whole page). The prune frees the empty pages once with `retain`.

Checks:

- New tests: a dead wrapper frees its key and its identity entries (this check fails when the `by_node` entry stays); a moved subtree keeps its expandos.
- Linux: `bare` lib 1640 passed; `bare-js` lib 1045 passed; `bare-js-api` 5 passed and 1 doc test. Windows 11 VM: 301 collect, wrapper, listener, event, shadow, template and select tests of `bare`, 141 owner, collect, host and weak tests of `bare-js`, and 5 tests of `bare-js-api` pass.

Closest row: `select_load churn 1000` +0.485% (glibc) and +0.498% (jemalloc). It makes and frees 20 021 wrappers; each one now costs a key, an owner entry and a prune step. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` abort on the base too.
- The first matrix run of this build showed a glibc mean of -7.5% with jemalloc near 0. The cached base counts were wrong (hypothesis: they came from another base build with the same mtime). A run with an empty cache gave the numbers above.

## 2026-11-19: host-filled properties by kind key (plan step S0.4, first PR)

Option A of `docs/design-lazy-properties.md`, with a change from the owner after the first build. See "Build of the first PR" in that document.

Changes:

- Engine: `Exotic::Indexed(key)` and `Exotic::Named(key)` hold a host key. `new_indexed`, `new_named` and `new_named_open` take it. The heap gives the object and its key to the source. `IndexedSource` and `NamedSource` take the key. `Heap::host_key(o)` gives it.
- `bare-js-api`: `Host` gets `indexed_len`, `indexed_item`, `indexed_name`, `indexed_names`, `named_has`, `named_get`, `named_len` and `named_keys`. Each gets the object and its key. New types: `Pending` (`Busy`, `Fill(index)`), `Item` and `Named`. `Interp::set_api_sources(host)` installs one adapter for both heap sources.
- `named_masking` is gone. An object of `new_named_open` gets a flag (`NAMED_OPEN`) in its header when it is made. The heap keeps the last named object and its key, so `realize` does not look up `exotics` again.
- Browser: `browser_sources.rs`. The key of a host-filled object is its kind (`Source`, 1 to 9). Ten creation sites use `Dom::new_source`. A read is one jump on the key, then the subsystem's own lookup by the object. The probe chains of the old `IndexedSource` and `NamedSource` impls of `Dom` are gone. `browser_frames::is_owner` is gone (only masking used it).
- The objects are not owners yet: no owner slot, no engine owner entry, no prune step.

| Kind in the key; the host gets the object | 4 | `dataset_load keys 10000 1` +1.26% |

## 2026-11-19: module cost row (plan step S0.4, MD0)

Added the `loader_load modules` case and its rows (`tools/js/cost_rows.txt`, scales 1 and 10; `tools/js/loader_load.sh` runs it too). No engine or browser code changed.

Case: `SCALE*20` inline module scripts. Each imports one of 4 mid modules. A mid module imports 2 of 4 leaf modules. A leaf imports `shared` through an import map entry. `shared` has a top-level await. A classic script makes `SCALE*10` `import()` calls of the mid modules. The checks compare `sum`, `sq`, the call counts, the `import()` sums and the single top-level await effect with the same computation in Rust. A mid module changed to `v * 3 + w` fails: `FAIL: checksum 870,0,20 != 700,0,20`, exit 1.

First design had 20*SCALE external root files. Its spread was 0.40% at scale 1 and 0.60% at scale 10: parallel loopback fetches change the count. Roots are inline now, and `import()` loads modules that are cached. Only 9 files are fetched, so the case is a cost row for parse, link, evaluate, import map and `import()`, and not for network.

Instruction counts (archMachine, `tools/js/instr.sh`, 5 runs of its min-of-3, glibc, release):

| `loader_load modules 10` | 29,165,849 | 29,186,772 | 0.072% |

It charges one step for each key.
