Reading:
- Per object the new cell is 3.1 times smaller than the old engine's (96.9 against 301.6 bytes with the shape bytes; 84.3 against 293.2 without them). Most of this is not the shapes: the old object is a 104-byte record with 16-byte values, and the new one is an 8-byte header with 8-byte values (S1.2, S1.4).
- Shapes cost more in the new engine: 276,276 bytes for 1,661 shapes (166 each) against 184,581 for 1,466 (126 each), +50% in bytes and +13% in count. Slack roots explain the count, not the bytes: the first 8 objects of a site get a root with the initial capacity and the later ones a root with the settled capacity (8 props objects, 8 fibers: a second 24-key chain). The same trace with fixed capacities (props 8, fibers 24; a scratch change of the example, not kept) gives 1,522 shapes and 270,805 bytes (178 each), so the slack roots add 139 shapes and 5,471 bytes. The bytes come from the size of the records: the node is 48 bytes, the table struct is 72, the entry vectors have 18% spare room (5,276 entries of room for 4,484), and a 24-entry dictionary has a node, a table, 24 entries and a 256-byte index (about 670 bytes by arithmetic: 48, 72, 288, 256; not measured on its own) against 1,689 bytes for the old dictionary. Hypothesis, not built: the dictionary fields (`free`, `tombs`, `dict`) of the table in an optional box would cut the table struct to 48 bytes (11 KB here), and `shrink_to_fit` on the entry vectors at the collection would cut the spare room (10 KB).
- Slack: the props site settles at 8 inline slots (the most that one of its first 8 objects used), but the objects use 4.5 on average. So 3.5 slots (28 bytes) of 80 bytes per props object are empty. The rule `max` is V8's. A site that makes objects of many shapes wastes the difference. Not changed; a rule with a percentile of the first 8 would give fewer inline slots and more overflow records (an overflow record is at least 32 bytes with its pointer word), so it needs a measurement on a real page.
- The old engine keeps the 1 in 16 props objects that delete their first key in shape mode (8 properties or fewer), and so does the new one. Only the 100 fibers go to dictionary mode in both.

## 2026-11-20: collector, ephemerons and weak tables (plan step S1.5)

`bare-js2` has a collector (`crates/js2/src/gc.rs`, design 6.9 item 3 and 6.11 item 3). `gc::collect(heap, shapes, atoms, roots)` runs one walk: `Heap::start_mark`, the roots, the mark loop, ephemerons, `Shapes::finish_marks`, `Atoms::sweep`, `Roots::weak`, `Heap::finish_mark`. The sweep stays lazy (S1.3).

- Roots are walked in place. A `Roots` impl (or a closure) calls `Marker::value` for each root where it lives. No root list is built. `Roots::weak(&Live)` is the hook for the weak tables of the host (a `WeakRef` target, the wrapper table): it runs after the marking and before the sweep.
- Mark bit before push: `Marker::cell` marks a cell and pushes it only when the mark was new. A cell with no edge (a flat string) is marked and never pushed. A shared atom (`FLAG_SHARED`) is skipped: it is in no heap of the realm.
- The work list is a stack of chunks of 256 entries (2 KiB). A chunk is allocated when the last one is full. An emptied chunk becomes the one spare, so a push and a pop at a chunk boundary do not allocate. The list never rescans the heap. It is dropped when the collection ends. Its peak is the number of cells found and not traced yet.
- The typed trace is one `match` on the layout in the header (`Marker::trace`). Arms: leaf strings (none), `Rope` and `Indirect` (`Str::children`), `Object` (the stub layout of S1.4: the header and one value slot for each slot of the stub `Shape`; every slot must hold a value from the allocation), and the new `Layout::WeakTable = 17`. S1.8 and S1.9 add their arms there.
- Ephemerons: a `WeakTable` is marked like any cell, and its keys are not edges. When the marker traces a table, an entry whose key is marked marks its value at once. Another entry waits in `Waiting` (a map from the key address to a chain of values; a value that is not a pointer waits for nothing). When the marker pops a cell and `Waiting` is not empty, it looks the cell up and marks the values. A leaf string cannot be a key, so leaves are never looked up. Each entry is looked at once and released at most once: the work is linear in the entries of the reachable tables, in any order. After the loop, an entry whose key is not marked is cleared (the key and value become `undefined`). A key that is only reachable through its own value dies. The stub layout of the table (header, `len: u32`, then `len` pairs of values) is for the tests; S1.9 may replace it.
- Weak atoms: `Atoms::sweep` runs after the marking (S1.7 hook). The shape table: `Shapes::finish_marks` runs before it (S1.4 hook).
- New in `heap.rs`: `Heap::marked_bytes()`, the bytes of the cells that the last `finish_mark` found marked (size class for a small cell, whole mapping for a large one). It counts the mark bits of each block (64 words) and costs about nothing. It is the "live bytes" of the leak test. New in `cell.rs`: the `WeakTable` layout code (one arm in `string.rs` for the match).

Checks (all on the head of this change):

- 15 new tests in `gc_tests.rs`; `bare-js2` has 50: Linux 50 pass, Windows 11 VM 50 pass (`cargo xwin test`), Miri (nightly 2026-11-17) 50 pass, 173 s wall for the whole crate (the S1.7 run was 143 s of test time; not split by test). Miri keeps the one known warning (integer-to-pointer cast of `Value::as_pointer`).
- Stress test with a random object graph (objects of 1 to 6 slots, flat strings, ropes, weak tables; edges at random; roots at 1 in 40): a model computes the kept set with the ephemeron rule by a fixpoint. After the collection the test checks: marked cells equal the model, no live cell is handed out again (60,000 nodes and 3 seeds, 20,000 new cells written over the freed memory), object ids, rope children and table entries are intact, entries of dead keys are cleared. A second collection of the same graph marks the same cells and bytes.
- No leaks: with only the pinned shape objects as roots, `marked_bytes` after the graph dies equals the start value, and `mapped_bytes` goes back to the start plus the pool of `POOL_KEEP` blocks. Also tested: a round test that grows the graph 6 times, a chain of 200,000 objects (no recursion), a chain of 20,000 tables in the worst order (`waited` = `released` = n - 1), cycles, an object that names its own key, a table reached only through the value of another, and the host weak hook.

Scratch of the collector (`tools/js/instr.sh`, min of 3; `crates/js2/examples/gc_load.rs`, release; archMachine, AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX; N = 1,000,000 objects of 40 bytes, cell class 48, live 48,000,016 bytes; the cost of R = 5 collections minus R = 0, divided by 5 and by N):

| Graph | Peak work list | Share of live bytes | Instructions per object | Cycles per object (1 run, shared machine) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `chain`: 1 link to the next object, 3 random links | 3,385,344 B (1,653 chunks) | 7.1% | 276 | 507 |
| `tree`: binary tree | 2,048 B (1 chunk) | 0.004% | 195 | 55 |
| stress test, 300,000 nodes, 16% live (from the test) | 45,056 B | 1.9% | n/a | n/a |

The mark bits are in the block headers: 512 bytes for each 64 KiB block (0.78%), fixed. The chain row is the worst case for the work list: a random graph with 4 links keeps a large frontier, at most 8 bytes for each cell found and not traced (at most 1/6 of the live bytes for 48-byte cells). Its cycles are latency: each link reads a header at a random address. A prefetch at the push is the usual remedy; not tried. I did not measure the scratch of the old collector on the same graph, so there is no old-against-new number here.

Where the instructions go (`perf record -e instructions:u`, tree, R = 20): `Marker::cell` 69%, `drain` (pop and trace) 26%, `Heap::sweep` 3%. About 16% of the samples of `cell` sit on the `div` in `Heap::mark` (the cell index is `offset / cell size`, a 64-bit division at the 64 KiB block header lookup).

Findings, not changed: (1) The division in `Heap::mark` and `is_marked` can become a multiply by a reciprocal kept in the block header (exact for offsets below 64 KiB). Not built or measured. (2) The stub `Shapes` has no sweep of its table: a dead shape id keeps a dangling entry. A cell made with a dead id would read a freed shape, so the tests pin one live object for each shape. S1.8 must decide the life of a shape. (3) A shape that names cells (S1.8) must be traced inside the loop of step 3 and 4, not after it: `finish_marks` only sets the mark bit. (4) A cell with many edges pushes all of them at once, so the peak of the work list is the edge count of the widest live cell. A long array (S1.9) may want a scan in slices. (5) `cargo clippy -p bare-js2 -- -D warnings` fails today in `bare-os` (`manual_is_multiple_of`, `pages.rs:19`) and warns in `heap.rs` (`manual_checked_ops`, lines 217 and 235). Neither is in this change.

Not tested: a collection inside a task or a trigger (S1.6); real object layouts, arrays and shapes (S1.8, S1.9); a realm that collects while a second realm reads a shared atom (only one realm in the tests); arm64; wall time and the cycle numbers on an idle machine; the cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser); the old collector's scratch on the same graph.
## 2026-11-20: clone_copy, the fused structured clone (design-host-clone.md step 5)

`structuredClone` and a same-heap `postMessage` with no transfer list now copy in one pass with no record. Linux and Windows pass the filtered tests. The cost matrix has no row over the limit. `web_apis_load clone` falls by about 10%, and `history` and `messages` are at or below the base. Base: origin/main `1cfb3807`, which has #741 (step 4). Since `d387c71f`, the head of #741 when I measured, main changed no file of `crates/bare`, `crates/js` or `crates/js-api` (`git diff --stat`). So all numbers below come from a fresh build of `d387c71f`, which has the same sources as the base.

Changes.

- `crates/js/src/eval_clone.rs`: `CloneCp` and `Interp::clone_copy_impl`, and `Engine::clone_copy` in `eval_api.rs`. The walk has the same checks, the same getter order and the same cost-model calls as `CloneWalk`. It makes the new object first, so a cycle finds it, walks the properties, and installs them at once with `clone_install` and `fill_array` (the step 4 paths and the same `CloneShapes`). No script can reach the new objects, so no getter sees a half-built copy. Strings and BigInts are immutable, so the copy shares them: no `str_units`, no intern, no limbs vector. A key is the source key. The steps that `clone_in` charged (1 for each object, key, element and map entry) are added up and charged when the copy is whole, so the total is the same and a failed walk charges none of them, as before.
- `crates/bare/src/browser_navigation_state.rs`: `clone_with` calls `clone_copy` when the transfer list is empty. A list keeps the record path. `clone_limits()` holds the three numbers once. `clone_payload` (`browser_scheduler.rs`) calls `clone_with` for an object message.
- `crates/js/src/heap_shape.rs`: `clone_prop` and `clone_elem` are `#[inline(always)]`. See "Layout" below.

Differential test: `clone_fast_path_gives_what_the_generic_path_gives` has 6 realms now. The 4 of step 4, then `clone_copy` with the fast paths off and with them on. All 6 must give the same copy, getter log, source graph after the walk, and cost or error, and the fused walk must take the fast path for the same objects as the walk. The generator has 0n and a heap BigInt now. 1,000 seeds by default. 20,000 seeds passed on the first version of the walk, 10,000 on the final one (15,398 fast objects, 748 half-way fallbacks, 480 throws, 2,895 limit or error stops). Two deliberate faults in `CloneCp` (a hole read as `null`, a missing sparse `length`) each failed it, so it sees an error in the new walk.

The one known difference (design risk 4): the engine heap ends the script while the copy is built. `clone_out` and `clone_in` run every getter first, then fail. `clone_copy` fails at the allocation, so a getter after that point has not run. `clone_copy_out_of_heap_stops_before_a_later_getter` gives both errors (the same) and the getter count (1 against 0). A heap limit is not catchable, so no page sees it. The same holds for the step budget: it ends at the end of the copy instead of between the two phases.

Layout. With the first version of the change `history 1` and `10` were +0.07% over the base (about 49 instructions a state), with the same result at codegen-units=1 on both trees (+0.065%, +0.071%). The history path runs code that this change did not touch. Callgrind with symbols showed `clone_prop` as 4,000 calls in the new build that the base had inlined: the second caller changed the inline choice. `#[inline(always)]` on `clone_prop` and `clone_elem` fixed it. `inline(always)` on the new helpers and a revert of the shared helper functions did not change the +0.07%, so they are not in the PR.

Measured: archMachine (AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX), release builds of the base (`/data/bare-tmp/s0/copy5-base-src`) and the PR. `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh -j4`, 3 runs a row, minimum of `instructions:u`. 819 rows, 817 measured. Mean change glibc -0.020%. No row over +0.5% under glibc (the largest are `date_load longstr 10` +0.101% and `longstr 1` +0.090%), so the jemalloc run and the codegen-units=1 rule did not apply to any row. `parse_load deep 1` and `10` fail on both trees (the known stale example). The rows of the brief, with jemalloc run on them (`-J`):

| Row | glibc base | glibc new | Change | jemalloc base | jemalloc new | Change |

## 2026-11-20: objects (plan step S1.9)

`bare-js2` has objects (`crates/js2/src/object.rs`; design 6.4, 6.9 items 5 and 8, 6.11 item 14). The collector traces them (`gc.rs`); the stub `Object` layout of S1.4 is gone. Base: origin/main after #745 (S1.8 shapes joined with the S1.5 collector).

What it has:
- Object cell. The header of `cell.rs` (shape id, layout code, flags), then inline value words. The layout `Object` has `cap` inline words, `cap` odd and at least `shape.inline()`; the layout `Indexed` (arrays, `arguments`) has the elements word after the header and an even `cap`. `cap` is `inline` rounded up so that the cell is a multiple of 16 bytes, which the allocator needs anyway: the rounding is free room. An empty object is 16 bytes; an object of 8 inline slots is 80 bytes and has 9 slots.
- Overflow record, only for an object that grows. No cell has a pointer word that it does not use. When an object gets more slots than `cap`, its last inline word holds the pointer to a `Slots` record and the value that was there moves to the record's first value (header flag `F_OVER`). Slot `i` is inline for `i < cap - 1` and `record[i - (cap - 1)]` after. For a tree shape the flag is set exactly when `shape.slots > cap`, so a cache that holds the shape knows where a slot is (S2 needs no flag read). A dictionary object may hold a record early. This is the answer to 6.11 item 14 (a pointer in every object, or reserved only in layouts that grow): it costs no byte in an object that does not grow, and it needs no choice of layout per allocation site. Growth is by half (first record: 4 values, at least what is needed), `Obj::new` for a shape that has the slots gives an exact record. A failed allocation leaves the object as it was.
- `Obj`: `new`, `slot`, `set_slot`, `add` (a transition, or a dictionary shape; accessors use 2 slots), `remove` (uses `Removed::shifts` of S1.8: the later slots move down; an object that fits its inline words again drops its record), `reconfigure` (attributes, data to accessor moves the property to fresh slots), `set_proto`.
- Elements in one tagged layout. The elements word points to an `Elements` record: header (capacity), `len`, `count`, then values. Every element is a `Value`, so integers, doubles and pointers need no other kind (6.9 item 8: no numeric-only store until an element census asks). A missing element is the new `Value::HOLE`. Dense form: value `i` is element `i`; `len` and `cap` are independent (`new Array(1e6)` is a record of capacity 0). Sparse form: sorted pairs (index, value), binary search. A write more than `DENSE_GAP` = 1,024 above the capacity makes it sparse; a sparse record that has one element in four of the indexes up to its last goes back to dense. Growth by half, literals exact. A plain `Object` has no elements word: its integer keys are properties of its shape (`ownKeys` order is for S3).
- Collector. The `Object` and `Indexed` arm scans the value words after the header (`object::words`); the pointer to the record and the elements word are ordinary edges. The arm `Slots | Elements` scans the capacity of a record (unused room holds holes and `undefined`, so every word is a valid value). A record of more than `SLICE` = 1,024 values is scanned in slices: the rest of the range waits in a small stack (`Marker::big`, 24 bytes per range) and the marker takes the next slice only when the work list is empty. `Stats::work_bytes` counts the stack.
- Small changes outside: `Layout::{Indexed, Slots, Elements}` and `CellHeader::record` (a record has no shape; the shape word holds its capacity) in `cell.rs`; one arm in `string.rs`; `Value::HOLE` in `value.rs`; the comment of the unsafe modules in `lib.rs`, `Cargo.toml` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (it listed `value`, `heap`, `string`, `atoms`; it now lists the modules that have `#[allow(unsafe_code)]`: `cell`, `heap`, `string`, `atoms`, `shapes`, `object`, `gc`; `value` has none). `gc_tests.rs` makes its objects with `Obj::new` (shapes of 8 inline slots; the wide-object test is now the slice test); `examples/gc_load.rs` does the same. `heap.rs` is not touched.

Layout census (M3), the same synthetic workload as S1.8 (`tools/js/shape_trace.js`, the React-like trace; 22,000 objects, all alive; deterministic, so 1 run each; archMachine). New: `object_census trace 1` makes the objects with `Obj::add`, `Site`, `Obj::remove`, and holds them in one array `keep` (as the script does). It sums size classes by kind and checks the sum against the live bytes of one collection (they are equal). Old: `BARE_JS_STATS=1 BARE_JS_EXEC=auto eval_check -e 'var SCALE = N; <shape_trace.js>'` (`tools/js/layout_census.sh` names the census; the numbers are the layout line at the end with SCALE 1 minus SCALE 0; `EVAL_CHECK_STEPS=4000000000`). Old buckets here were counted again and agree with S1.8.

New bytes per object, by kind (size classes of the cell and its record): props 79.9 (8,000 objects; 4.5 slots on average), element 64.0 (8,000; 6 slots), hook 48.0 (4,000; 5 slots), fiber 255.9 (2,000; 24 slots; 100 in dictionary mode). The old census has no split by kind.

| Per object (22,000) | New | Old, `auto` | Old, `tree` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| objects, slots, dictionaries | 84.3 | 293.2 | 291.2 |
| plus the array `keep` (new: 262,144 bytes, capacity 27,310; old: `elements`, 524,288 bytes) | 96.2 | 317.0 | 314.1 |
| plus the shapes (new: 276,451 bytes, 1,663 shapes; old: 184,581 and 184,043) | 108.8 | 325.4 | 322.5 |

- The new object side is 3.3 times smaller than the old one with the array (96.2 against 317.0) and 3.0 times with the shapes (108.8 against 325.4). The numbers of S1.8 were a model; the real objects give the same bytes (84.3 per object; props 79.9, element 64.0, hook 48.0, fiber 255.9), so the model was right. 8 fibers and 2 props objects have an overflow record (the first objects of their sites); the rest fit their inline words.
- Slack, not changed: a props object has 4.5 of its 9 words in use on average, so about 36 of its 80 bytes are empty. Hypothesis, not built: a percentile of the first 8 objects instead of their maximum would cut the inline words and add overflow records of at least 32 bytes.
- Shapes cost more than in the old engine (166 bytes each against 126, and 1,663 shapes against 1,466); the S1.8 notes on this are unchanged.

Arrays (`object_census array N`; old: `tools/js/array_trace.js` with `var KIND`, same method; N = 100,000 for both; the new engine also at N = 1,000,000):

| Workload | New, bytes per item | Old, `auto` | Old, `tree` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| N arrays `[i, i+1, i+2]` in one array | 91.1 (cell 32, record 48, and the slot in the outer array) | 235.8 | 219.8 |
| N integers pushed to one array | 11.1 (capacity 138,255: 1.5 growth) | 21.0 | 21.0 |
| N empty objects in one array | 27.1 (object 16, slot in the array) | 171.8 | 171.8 |

At N = 1,000,000 the new rows are 88.5, 8.45 and 24.45 bytes per item. The mapping of a large cell is a multiple of 64 KiB, so the pushed-integer array at N = 1,000,000 (capacity 1,049,869) has 8,454,176 live bytes: a record of 129 blocks and the 32-byte cell.

Work list on a 1M-element array (`object_census array 1000000`, one array of 1,000,000 object elements, 24,454,176 live bytes): with slices (`SLICE` = 1,024) `work_bytes` is 10,264 (0.04% of the live bytes); with the slicing switched off (a scratch build, `SLICE` = `usize::MAX / 2`, not kept) it is 8,001,536 (32.7%), the 8 bytes for each element that the record pushes at once. The slice test in `gc_tests.rs` asserts the bound for a record of 16,394 values.

Collector rows (`gc_load`, release, `tools/js/instr.sh` minimum of 3 runs, 10 collections minus 0, divided by 10 and by N = 100,000 objects of 4 slots; both objects are 48-byte cells; base = the head of #745 built from its own checkout):

| Row | Before (stub arm) | After (object arm) | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `chain` | 284.3 per object | 255.3 | -10.2% |
| `tree` | 201.5 | 196.5 | -2.5% |

The setup rows (R = 0) are 11.7 M and 33.6 M for `chain` (the new setup makes the objects through `Obj::new` and `set_slot`), so the rows are not comparable in setup, only in the collection. Why the collection is cheaper is not known (hypothesis: the stub arm read `shapes.of(h).slots` and the new one reads the inline capacity of the same record; not measured by a profile). Peak work list is unchanged (2,048 bytes for `tree`).

Micro rows (`crates/js2/examples/object_load.rs`; release; user instructions from `perf stat` through `tools/js/instr.sh`, N = 1,000,000 minus N = 0; the instruction counts do not vary between runs):

| Row | Instructions per op |
| --- | ---: |
| `new` (alloc, header, 5 words filled; no collection) | 88 |
| `add` (a property of an object whose transitions exist; `(add row - new row) / 4`) | 170 |
| `slot`, inline (loop with no object: 16, so about 30) | 46 |
| `slot`, in the record (24 properties, 8 inline; about 48 net) | 64 |
| `get_element`, dense (about 41 net) | 57 |
| `set_element` at the end (push; growth included) | 58 |

These are for native reads and writes. A cache hit in S2 does not call `slot`: it compares the shape id and loads the word at a fixed offset (for a record slot, one more load). `add` includes a shape transition (about 28), the check for room, the header write and the slot write; not tuned.

Checks: `bare-js2` has 93 tests: Linux 93 pass; Windows 11 VM 93 pass (`cargo xwin test`, `bare_js2` exe through `winssh`); Miri (nightly): 93 pass in 567 s of test time (the one known integer-to-pointer warning of `Value::as_pointer`). 24 new tests in `object_tests.rs`: geometry; the free room of the rounding; every value across the inline/record boundary at every step for 5 capacities; record growth; an accessor that straddles the boundary; delete of the last key, of a middle key (the shape equals that of an object that never had the key), and the fall back into the inline words; a dictionary object with slot reuse; attribute change and data to accessor; prototype change; elements (literal, push, holes, delete, length, `new Array(1e6)`, sparse and dense again); a random test of 6 seeds against a `BTreeMap` (writes, deletes, length changes, pushes, indexes in three ranges); the collector (inline slots, record, dense and sparse elements, a record that the object outgrew, a long array in slices with truncation, a sparse record longer than a slice); `from_value` refuses a record. 1 test of `gc_tests.rs` changed (the wide object is scanned in slices); the others only changed their object maker.

Not tested: arm64; a 32-bit target; the cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser); a collection inside a task (S1.6); a cache that uses the layout (S2); typed arrays, `arguments` and exotic objects (no layout for them yet); an element census on a real page (the arrays here are synthetic; no numeric-only elements store was built, as 6.9 item 8 says); an allocation failure (`Heap::alloc` returning `None` has no hook to force it); `Obj::add` and `remove` under a shape cap; a dictionary object that holds a record early (tested only through slot reuse); the examples on the Windows VM; wall time.

Lines that name `Interp`, `Value`, `ObjId` or `it.`: 6,851 of 66,560 (10.3%). `s.engine()`: 6 sites in 2 files.

## 2026-11-20: collection inside a task (plan step S1.6)

`bare-js2` collects inside a task: the allocation slow path refuses at a trigger, and the allocation helper collects with the frames as roots (design 6.8, 6.11 item 1, section 10 Q11). Base: the S1.8 branch (#745, `af044070`), because #745 was still open. New: `crates/js2/src/roots.rs` (root maps, frame stack, `alloc_in_task`). Changed: the allocation slow path in `heap.rs`, and `gc.rs` (one `Marker::shape` method and one doc line).

The trigger:
- `Heap` counts the bytes of cells that the allocator took since the last collection (`grown_bytes`). The count grows on the slow path only, when a block (new, from the pool, or swept) gives its free cells to the free list. The fast path of `alloc` has no counter and no compare. The count runs ahead of the real allocation by at most the cells of one refilled block for each class, so the trigger has the resolution of a block (64 KiB).
- Two limits, both reset by `finish_mark`. `Heap::due()` is the limit between tasks: the old rule of `Interp::gc_due`, written as growth: the heap (live bytes of the last collection plus growth) passes the larger of 8 MiB and 1.75 times the live bytes. `Heap::try_alloc` refuses on its slow path at that limit plus `slack` (8 MiB). `try_alloc` has the same fast path as `alloc`. `alloc` never refuses. `Trigger { min, slack }` and `Heap::set_trigger` set the sizes.
- How the sizes were chosen. `task_alloc_max` (P0.2, section "collector counters" above): the typing page 4,388,944 B (4.19 MiB), the staging journey 4,227,240 B at most in 3 runs of 4 realms. A task starts with growth below the between-task limit (the host collects at the safepoint when `due()`), so it reaches the task limit only if it grows by more than the slack. The slack of 8 MiB is 1.9 times the largest measured task: no task on those workloads collects inside itself, and the roots of the frames are not walked there. `min` of 8 MiB is `GC_MIN_BYTES` of the old engine; the factor 1.75 is its tuned value (`decisions.md`). A task that makes garbage in a loop (`eval_load throws`, 32.4 MiB peak on the old engine) collects at about 16 MiB of growth, then again every 16 MiB. Hypothesis: that is the peak there. The new engine runs no script yet, so this is not measured. A lower slack costs more collections and more exposure to a wrong root map; the slack is one constant.
- `alloc_in_task(heap, shapes, atoms, roots, size)`: `try_alloc`; if it refuses, `collect` (when the task limit has passed), then `alloc`. The collection runs before the cell exists, so the new cell needs no root. The cold part is a separate function.

Root maps and frames (`roots.rs`):
- `RootMaps` is the data of one function: for each safepoint (its `pc`), a bitmap of the registers that hold a live, written value. One `Vec<u64>` of `regs.div_ceil(64)` words for each safepoint, and one `Vec<u32>` of `pc`s that the compiler adds in increasing order. `find(pc)` is a binary search. Slots of a map come out by `trailing_zeros`: the cost is the words and the live registers. I chose a bitmap over a list of register numbers: a frame of 32 registers takes 4 bytes against 2 bytes for each live register. A list wins only when a frame has more than 16 registers for each live one. Safepoints with the same map are not shared; S2 decides that when it knows the compile-time bytes.
- No frame stores its map. A frame stores `pc`; the lookup runs only in a collection. So the maps cost no run-time work until a collection (design 6.11 item 1).
- `Frames` is the JS stack: one `Vec<Value>` for the registers of all frames, a record `{code, pc, base}` for each frame (design 6.10 item 8). `push` does not clear the registers: a new frame sees what an earlier frame wrote (design 6.10 item 4). The collector reads only the registers that the map names, so a stale register may hold the pointer of a freed cell. `push_native` makes a frame of `undefined` registers that are all roots: the scoped roots of host code (design 6.8).
- `Frames::walk(&self, marker, codes)` marks each live register where it is stored. It makes no list of roots. It is the body of `Roots::walk` for a realm. A safepoint with no map panics: skipping the frame would free values that the program reads. A caller frame is walked at the `pc` of its call, the top frame at the `pc` of its allocation. The register that the allocation writes is not live at that `pc`.
- `Marker::shape(id)` (new, `gc.rs`) keeps a shape that no marked object has yet, and marks its prototype. A shape that code or a native function holds before it makes the first object is otherwise freed by `Shapes::finish_marks`, and its id may name another shape later. Found while writing the roots: S1.8's note says "valid until the next `finish_marks`", and an in-task collection makes that point reachable inside one operation. Rule for S1.9 and S2: allocate the cell first and make the shape after it, or pin the shape in the roots.
- Rule: no raw cell pointer lives in a Rust local or `Vec` across a call that can collect (`alloc_in_task` and everything that calls it). It is in a frame or a native frame, or it is not kept.

Checks:
- 14 new tests in `roots_tests.rs` (9) and `heap_tests.rs` (5); `bare-js2` has 82: Linux 82 pass, Windows 11 VM 82 pass (`cargo xwin test`, 7.3 s). Miri (nightly 2026-11-17), filter `roots` and `heap::tests` (19 tests): 19 pass, 187 s; the whole crate was not run again under Miri.
- The check of the plan step (`a_collection_in_a_task_keeps_the_live_registers_and_frees_the_dead_ones`): three frames (a caller, a callee, a native frame) with live objects in a cycle, and dead objects in the registers that the map does not name. Before the frames exist, the stack holds the pointers of 13 objects that a collection freed, so the unlisted registers hold stale pointers. After the collection: 6 cells marked (no stale register was read), `marked_bytes` is the 6 objects and the two key atoms, each dead cell is handed out again by the next allocations, no live cell is, and after the free cells are overwritten the live objects keep every value and edge. With the walk changed to read all registers, this test fails; with the frame walk removed, it fails.
- Trigger tests: the count grows by the free cells of a block and not at each cell (fast path counts nothing); a swept block counts only its free cells; `due()` follows the old rule (floor, and 0.75 times 1 MiB live); `try_alloc` refuses at the task limit for small and large requests while `alloc` does not; a collection lifts the refusal; `set_trigger` with 0 and with `usize::MAX`.
- Task tests: 400,000 objects through `alloc_in_task` (a list that grows and is cut every 50, a long-lived object, a dead register with a stale pointer): 21 collections, the list is whole at the end, mapped bytes stay near the limits, and the last collection kept at most 53 objects. A task below the limit does not walk the roots. A pinned shape with no object survives, with its prototype; an unpinned one is freed.

Cost of the trigger on the allocation fast path (`crates/js2/examples/heap_load.rs`, release, `tools/js/instr.sh` = minimum of 3 runs, repeated 3 times, archMachine, AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX, load about 2.5; base `af044070`; N = 20,000,000 allocations of 32 bytes in rounds of 100,000, minus N = 0):

| Row | Instructions per allocation (3 repeats) |
| --- | ---: |
| base `heap` | 23.388, 23.388, 23.387 |
| new `heap` | 23.393, 23.393, 23.393 |
| new `try` (`Heap::try_alloc`) | 23.395, 23.395, 23.395 |

- The fast path is the same code: `alloc` and `try_alloc` pop the free list and nothing else. The new `heap` row is +0.006 instructions per allocation (+0.024%): the counting on the slow path, about 11 instructions for each block that is refilled (a popcount of the 64 mark words). `try` is +0.002 over `heap` (+0.007%).
- `task` mode (new): 20,000,000 objects of 2 slots through `alloc_in_task`, the last 1,000 in a native frame, the trigger collects (38 collections): 67.2 instructions per allocation, of which the loop itself (shape header, 3 stores, the frame write) is most. `perf record` (1 run): `finish_mark`, `Marker::cell`, `alloc_slow` and `sweep` together are 0.9% of the samples. A collection costs little here because only 1,000 objects are live; this row does not size the root walk of a deep stack. `alloc_in_task` and `Frames::regs` are not inlined across crates without `#[inline]`: the first build of the row had 106 instructions per allocation for that reason; both are `#[inline]` now.

Not tested: a real interpreter, compiler root maps or deep stacks (S2); a collection that a host function causes while JS frames are below it (the handle scopes of design 6.8 are one native frame here); the cost of a walk of a deep stack; the trigger on `eval_load throws` or on the journeys (the new engine runs no script, so the peak of 16 MiB there is arithmetic); a second realm; arm64; the cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser); wall time.

## 2026-11-20: lexer in js2 (plan step S2.1)

`bare-js2` has the lexer (`crates/js2/src/lex.rs`, tests in `lex_tests.rs`; design 6.9 item 9). It is the streaming lexer of `crates/js/src/lex.rs` with the same token type, goals, errors and decode helpers. A token is 12 bytes: a kind, a byte span into the source and two flags. The lexer borrows the source and never allocates while it scans. Base: origin/main `e36a8dd4`. `crates/js` is not changed.

Decision: the lexer gives spans, and the S2.5 compiler makes atoms. Reasons: (1) The lexer has no heap and no `Atoms`. With `Atoms` it would need `&mut Heap` and a realm, and an allocation failure path (`R<Str>`), in a loop that is allocation-free today (`lex_load` checks 0 allocations). (2) The grammar will also run in check-only mode (design 6.9 item 9) and skip nested functions. Most identifiers in such a text are never used as names, so interning them in the lexer is work that nothing needs. The compiler knows which names it needs (and a token with no escape is already a `&str` slice, `ident_name`). (3) `SharedAtoms::intern` takes a mutex. The compiler can intern once for each distinct name of a function, not once for each token. (4) A string literal can hold lone surrogates, so its value is `Vec<u16>` (`decode_string`), not text. The compiler decides which of them are keys (atoms) and which are only values. Cost of the choice: the compiler hashes a name that the lexer has already scanned. `Chars::One` takes a `&[u8]`, so a name with no escape can be passed as a slice of the source (to verify in S2.5).

What changed in the copy, and why:
- `use crate::number` is gone: `crates/js2` must not depend on `crates/js`. The three functions the lexer uses (`decimal_value`, `separated_decimal_value`, `reduce` with its helpers, about 110 lines of `number.rs`) are copied into `lex.rs` as private items. `decimal_units_value` (used only by the JSON parser) is not copied. When S2 gets a `Number(string)` conversion, it can take these from `lex.rs`.
- `icu_properties` (version, features and `compiled_data` as in `bare-js`) is a dependency of `bare-js2` for ID_Start and ID_Continue. Because of it the `license` field of `bare-js2` is now `(MIT OR Apache-2.0) AND Unicode-3.0` (the `bare-js` string without its `BSD-3-Clause` part; I did not check where that part comes from). `Cargo.lock` gets one line. `--locked` needs this line.
- The 31 tests moved to `lex_tests.rs` (`#[path]` module, as `atoms_tests.rs`), with one level less indent. No test changed.

- No `unsafe` in `lex.rs`: `#![deny(unsafe_code)]` of the crate holds, and the module has no `allow`. The old lexer has none either, so no measured gain was needed.

## 2026-11-20: sticky-mark young generation, experiment not kept (plan step S1.10)

The experiment is built and measured. It is **not kept in main**. The code is on branch `t3/js2-sticky-mark-minor-gc` (head `1f0a3eeb`, on top of the S1.9 branch `t3/js2-object-layout` at `bf367cb6`, PR #749). This entry is the only change in this PR.

What the experiment builds (`crates/js2`):
- Sticky marks. A collection no longer clears the mark bits of live cells. `Heap::sweep` keeps them. A marked cell is old. A full collection clears all marks first.
- Header flags `F_OLD` and `F_REM` (bits 22 and 23). The marker sets `F_OLD` on each non-leaf cell that it marks. The barrier tests it.
- Write barrier: `heap::barrier(holder, header, value, at)`. A store of a pointer into an old cell remembers the cell. A small cell gets `F_REM` (once) and a bit in a new `dirty` map in its block header (512 bytes more for each 64 KiB block). A long record (a large cell) has no flag. It gets a dirty bit for the card of the store (512 bytes, more for records over 2 MiB).
- Barrier sites: `Obj::set_slot`, element stores (`put_b`), the elements word, the overflow record pointer in `reserve`, the move in `remove`, a shape change (`set_shape`: the shape holds a prototype cell), and the rope flatten in `string.rs`.
- `gc::collect_minor`: roots, the prototype of every shape, the remembered cells and cards, then the mark loop. It marks only cells that are not marked. Shapes, runtime atoms and old cells are not freed. A full collection does that. `Shapes::clear_live` runs at the start of a full collection (a stale bit from a minor would skip the prototype mark). A new atom is marked when it is made, so a minor needs no walk of the atom table or of the shape keys.
- 4 new tests in `gc_tests.rs`: a store into an old object; records, elements, ropes and shape changes; cards of a long record (5,000 and 300,000 elements); a random graph of 8 seeds with minor and full collections and a model (freed cells are overwritten before the check). With the barrier switched off, 3 of them fail. `bare-js2` has 110 tests: Linux 110 pass. Miri (nightly 2026-11-17) on the 4 new tests: 4 pass, 262 s (the one known integer-to-pointer warning).
- Rows: `examples/barrier_load.rs` and `examples/gen_load.rs`.

Machine: archMachine, AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX, release builds, load 5 to 6. Counts are user instructions from `perf stat -e instructions:u` (3 runs; the spread is under 0.003% on every row below, so one number is given). Base tree: `bf367cb6` built in its own checkout.

### (a) Barrier cost for each store

`barrier_load`, N = 1,000,000 minus N = 0, instructions per operation including the loop (4):

| Row | Base | Experiment | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `Obj::set_slot`, young object, pointer | 42 | 62 | +20 |
| `Obj::set_slot`, old object, integer | 45 | 69 | +24 |
| `Obj::set_slot`, old object, pointer, already remembered | 42 | 62 | +20 |
| first pointer store into an old object (the object is remembered) | 38 | 91 | +53 |
| `set_element`, young array, pointer | 59 | 62 | +3 |
| `set_element`, old array of 4,096, pointer (every store records its card) | 59 | 104 | +45 |

- The check in the code is 3 instructions (flag test and branch). The `set_slot` rows grow by 20 because the function is not inlined into the loop, and the header and the value must stay in registers across `geometry`. In `gen_load` the function is inlined: the difference of 4,000,000 objects with 4 stores each (no collection) is 20.2 M instructions, 1.26 for each store. A record store is +2 to +3 when the array is young.
- Hypothesis: an inline cache hit in S2 pays the 3 to 5 instructions of the inline case and not the 20. Not measured.
- The record row is the weak point: a long record has no `F_REM`, so each store into an old record calls `remember`. A precomputed shift in the block header would cut it. Not built.

### (b) Collections and totals

Workload (`gen_load`, 200 rounds of 20,000 objects of 4 slots, 48 bytes each, 4 stores each, 200 stores of a young pointer into a kept object for each round): a share SURV of the new objects is kept in a ring array. A kept object dies when its ring slot is overwritten, LIFE rounds later. STATIC objects (a binary tree) are old data from the start.
- Survival rate used: 22% (the typing page, 96,567 of 438,033 young objects in the first collect) and 34% (the staging journey, 32.2% to 34.0%), both from the P0.2 entry (2026-11-18). Two more rows: 5% (the textbook case) and 34% with LIFE 40 (survivors live long).
- P0.2 measured only the first collect, not how long the survivors live. LIFE 3 means a survivor of a 2 MiB nursery dies a round or two after it is promoted. This is an assumption, not a measurement.
- Old data: the typing page has 12.6 MiB of live heap after load in the old engine (`progress.md`, entry on the shape work: "Alloc live after load: 17.0 MiB to 12.6 MiB"). The S1.9 layout is about 3.3 times smaller, so about 3.8 MiB. STATIC = 100,000 objects (4.8 MB) is the nearest row. STATIC = 0 and 400,000 (19 MB) bound it.
- Base policy: a full collection between rounds when `Heap::due()` (8 MiB, 1.75 times the live bytes). Experiment policy `gen`: a minor collection each 2 MiB of growth (nursery), a full one when the old bytes plus a nursery pass the limit of `due()`. The mutator code is the same.

Total instructions (millions), base `full` against experiment `gen`; "collection" is the total minus the same run with no collection (base) so the experiment's number includes the barrier and the sticky overhead:

| SURV, LIFE | STATIC | Base `full` | Experiment `gen` | Change | Collection, base to experiment | Minors / fulls | Peak mapped MiB, base / experiment |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 22%, 3 | 0 | 1,150.1 | 1,379.4 | +19.9% | 72.2 to 301.5 | 61 / 6 | 8.9 / 10.1 |
| 22%, 3 | 100,000 | 1,886.8 | 1,683.9 | -10.7% | 768.5 to 565.7 | 54 / 13 | 10.8 / 10.8 |
| 22%, 3 | 400,000 | 2,060.1 | 2,008.3 | -2.5% | 820.9 to 769.1 | 64 / 3 | 34.8 / 35.2 |
| 34%, 3 | 0 | 1,211.2 | 1,524.0 | +25.8% | 103.5 to 416.3 | 58 / 9 | 9.3 / 9.9 |
| 34%, 3 | 100,000 | 1,965.3 | 1,907.8 | -2.9% | 817.3 to 759.8 | 50 / 17 | 11.1 / 11.6 |
| 34%, 3 | 400,000 | 2,104.6 | 2,217.7 | +5.4% | 835.7 to 948.8 | 63 / 4 | 35.1 / 35.9 |
| 34%, 40 | 0 | 1,903.4 | 1,946.8 | +2.3% | 794.9 to 838.3 | 62 / 7 | 27.0 / 27.4 |
| 34%, 40 | 100,000 | 2,054.8 | 2,143.9 | +4.3% | 906.1 to 995.1 | 63 / 7 | 34.4 / 35.9 |
| 34%, 40 | 400,000 | 2,155.0 | 2,417.7 | +12.2% | 885.3 to 1,148.0 | 66 / 3 | 59.3 / 60.2 |
| 5%, 3 | 0 | 1,061.3 | 1,174.7 | +10.7% | 25.5 to 138.9 | 66 / 1 | 9.2 / 9.7 |
| 5%, 3 | 100,000 | 1,947.6 | 1,345.9 | -30.9% | 871.5 to 269.8 | 62 / 5 | 9.2 / 9.6 |
| 5%, 3 | 400,000 | 1,996.6 | 1,608.8 | -19.4% | 799.6 to 411.8 | 67 / 0 | 34.1 / 31.4 |

Nursery size, STATIC = 100,000 (total against base `full`): 1 MiB: -9.9%, -3.1%, +8.0%, -32.0%; 2 MiB: -10.8%, -2.9%, +4.3%, -30.9%; 4 MiB: -9.1%, -7.2%, -2.0%, -1.6% (rows in the order 22%/3, 34%/3, 34%/40, 5%/3; at 4 MiB the 5% row runs 40 full collections and no minor, so it is the base policy plus the barrier).

Cost of one collection at the same cadence (a collection each 2 MiB of growth; `minor` policy never runs a full collection):

| Row | Full collection | Minor collection |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 22%, 3, STATIC 100,000 | 22.9 M (113,138 cells marked) | 8.1 M (13,023 marked, 396 remembered) |
| 34%, 3, STATIC 100,000 | 24.6 M (120,302) | 11.8 M (20,141) |
| 34%, 40, STATIC 100,000 | 69.4 M (338,684) | 11.7 M (19,307) |
| 5%, 3, STATIC 100,000 | 20.3 M (102,991) | 3.0 M (2,968) |
| 22%, 3, STATIC 0 | 3.8 M (13,138) | 7.3 M (13,023) |
| 5%, 3, STATIC 0 | 1.3 M (2,991) | 2.1 M (2,968) |

- With old data of 4.8 MB a minor is 2 to 7 times cheaper than a full collection. With no old data a minor is 1.7 to 1.9 times dearer: it marks the same cells and pays for more bookkeeping. Hypothesis, from the sample counts of one `perf record`: the `minor` policy never frees old garbage (9 to 74 MiB at the end), and the lazy sweep then walks old blocks that have no free cell each time the allocator needs cells. Not isolated.
- A full collection costs more than in the base tree. `perf record` of `full`, 22%, 3, STATIC 100,000 (1 run): the mark functions 812 M samples against 723 M (+12%). The header write of `F_OLD` made `Marker::cell` too big to inline (+20% before `#[inline(always)]`). The rest of the excess in the `full` rows is the barrier on the old ring record (`remember`: 65 M).
- Whole-record remembering first gave +31% on 34%, 40 (a dirty record of 272,000 elements was scanned in each minor: `drain` 879 M). Cards cut it to +4%. The table has the card build only; the whole-record numbers are from one earlier run of the same matrix.
- Peak bytes: with STATIC 100,000 or more the experiment peaks 0 to 4.5% above the base, and in one row 8% below (5%, 400,000). With STATIC 0 it peaks 1.5% to 13% above. The end state holds floating garbage: at the end of 22%, 3, STATIC 100,000 the old bytes are 7.2 MiB against 5.4 MiB live. The dirty map takes 512 bytes of each 64 KiB block (0.8% fewer cells).

### Decision

Not kept. The rule was: keep it only if the barrier on all stores plus the collections cost less on workloads shaped like P0.2. The total is lower in 5 of 12 rows (all at 22% to 5% survival with old data of 4.8 MB or more, up to -30.9%) and higher in 7 (up to +25.8%). At the survival of the P0.2 rows (22% and 34%) the gain is 2.5% to 10.7% where it exists, on a toy mutator where collection is half of all instructions. A real mutator makes the share of the gain smaller. With no old data the 22% and 34% rows lose 20% and 26%. Costs that are not in the totals: a barrier on every store of S2 and of any later tier, a flag write per marked cell, a dirty map in each block, and the rule that every pointer store site needs the barrier. There are more sites than slot and element stores: the move in `remove`, `set_shape`, the rope flatten and the overflow pointer all needed one.

What would change the answer: a measured lifetime of survivors (how many of the 22% to 34% die in the next collect), and the old-data size of the real journeys on the new engine. Both need S2 or S3 to run script. Until then the base design (non-generational, lazy sweep) stays.

Findings, not changed in main: (1) A block with no free cell is swept again in each cycle; a minor collection could keep such blocks aside. Not built. (2) `remember` for a long record can be about 3 instructions with the shift kept in the block header. Not built. (3) The division in `Heap::mark` (S1.5 finding) is on every mark, minor or full. Not built.

Not tested: Windows (the experiment is not in main, so no VM run); a real interpreter or a JIT (the barrier in an inline cache, 3 to 5 instructions, is not measured); lifetimes of real survivors; the old-data size of the real journeys; arm64; wall time and cycles; weak tables in a minor collection beyond the stub (a table is traced when remembered; no test writes one after it is old); `Obj::add` under a shape cap with a remembered object; the cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser).

## 2026-11-20: parse-ahead with a claim table (plan step S2.3)

Change: new module `crates/js2/src/parse_ahead.rs` (tests in `parse_ahead_tests.rs`), one `pub mod` line in `lib.rs`. The module is generic over the parse step (`trait Job`: the mode, the result and `run`). It does not depend on the S2.2 parser. Std only. No `unsafe`.

- Identity: `Identity::of(text)` is the hash (the hash of the old `parse_cache`) and the length. The caller computes it once and passes it to `Sender::submit(mode, id, text)`. The result carries it (`Published::id`), so the compile step and the shared-code lookup (design 6.10 item 19) do not hash the text again. `Published::is(text)` compares the bytes (hash collision).
- Claim: the table is keyed by (identity, mode). A submit that finds the key only counts a waiter and returns a handle (`Pending`). It copies nothing and allocates nothing. A submit that finds no key claims it with a small slot, and copies the text after that, outside the lock. This fixes the review note about `parse_ahead.rs:151` (design 6.11): the old code copied the text and allocated a job before it looked for a queued duplicate.
- States: `Claimed`, `Queued` (holds the one copy of the text), `Running`, `Done`. One worker thread runs jobs and publishes. It ends after `Job::PARK` (2 s) idle, and starts again at the next job.
- Cancel: the last waiter that goes (drop of the last `Pending`, or `take` of queued work) removes a queued entry from the table and the queue. A running entry stays, and a new submit may join it. If no waiter is left when the job ends, the result is dropped (unpublished). `Ahead::cancel` (also on drop) empties the table and the queue, wakes every blocked waiter (`None`) and unpublishes the running job. A job that panics gives `None` and the worker goes on.
- `Pending::take` (for the page thread) waits for a running job but not for queued work (it cancels it and the caller parses). `Pending::wait` also waits for queued work.
- Results stay in the table while a handle is held. Later duplicates are for the cache of the caller: `Job::cached(mode, id)` is asked before the claim (the old `parse_cache::known`).
- Differences from the old module: no thread-local `attach` or `take` by hash (the handle replaces them); the hand-over needs no `unsafe Send` wrapper because the result must be `Send + Sync`; the entries leave with the last waiter.

Found by the flake loop: `take` on queued work removed the entry but did not wake a thread that blocked in `wait` on the same entry. That thread slept for ever (the stress test hung in run 46 of one loop; a second loop of 400 runs had no hang after the fix). Fixed with a `notify_all`, and a test for it (`a_take_of_queued_work_wakes_a_waiter_of_the_same_entry`). After the fix: 400 runs in a row, no failure.

Checks (20 tests): duplicate submits (same mode while queued and while running, other mode, after publish, 10 handles of one entry), cancel while queued (last waiter, `take`), cancel while running (unpublished, and a waiter that comes back), cancel by the page (queued work, running job, blocked waiter, owner drop), a panic, idle end and restart, the limits and `cached`, 16 threads that submit one source in 2 modes (20 rounds: 2 parses and 2 claims each), a stress of 8 threads that submit, take, wait and drop at once on a 4 MiB text (the copy overlaps with joins and takes), and no entry left after any of these.

| Where | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Linux, debug, `cargo test -p bare-js2 --lib parse_ahead` | 20 pass, 0.2 to 0.5 s |
| Linux flake loop (script: test binary 50 times in a row, then 25 rounds of 8 binaries at once), debug | 0 failures in 50 and in 200 parallel runs |
| Linux flake loop, release | 0 failures in 50 and in 200 parallel runs |
| Windows 11 VM (`cargo xwin test`, exe through `winssh`) | 20 pass; 50 runs in a row and 10 rounds of 6 at once: 0 failures |

Cost (archMachine, AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX, release, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, 3 runs each, the 3 runs agree within 0.01%; scratch crate `/data/bare-tmp/s0/ahead/bench` with both modules, not in the repo). Cost of one duplicate submit of a text that is already queued, running or done = (N duplicates minus N = 0) / N, minimum of 3. The old path is `bare_js::parse_ahead::Sender::submit`. It hashes the text, asks the cache, copies the text, allocates a slot, then finds the key.

| Text | Old submit | New, hash at each call (same work) | New, identity carried |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB (N = 2000) | 37,818 | 31,529 | 725 |
| 1 MiB (N = 200) | 590,781 | 492,329 | 724 |

- The hash is most of the cost of a duplicate when the caller computes it at each call: the new path saves the copy and the allocation (-17%). With the identity carried, a duplicate costs 725 instructions (a lock, a table lookup, an `Arc`-like handle, and the drop of the handle with a second lookup), 52 times fewer at 64 KiB and 816 times fewer at 1 MiB. The 725 are not a target: SipHash of the key is about a third of them. A pass-through hasher is possible if a profile ever asks.
- Memory for a queued job (live bytes, counted on the submitting thread, 200 jobs of 64 KiB and of 20,000 bytes, worker blocked): old 65,731 (2 allocations, 195 bytes over the text); new 65,744 (1 allocation, 208 bytes over the text, and this includes the 40-byte handle that the new API gives to the caller). The same within 13 bytes. The slot sits in the table, so the new path has one allocation for each job.

Not tested: the S2.2 parser as the job (the module takes any `Job`); wiring into the loader (`crates/bare`) or a cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser); a job that polls for cancel (the module cannot interrupt a running job; a job may later get a flag); Miri (the module has no `unsafe`; the crate's Miri run was not repeated); the body of a real page (many scripts, byte budget for held results: results stay until the handle goes or the page ends, without a cap); macOS.
## 2026-11-20: pre-parser in js2 (plan step S2.2)

`bare-js2` has a parser with a pre-parse mode (`crates/js2/src/parse.rs`, `ast.rs`, `facts.rs`; design 6.5 and 6.9 items 4 and 9). Base: the S2.1 branch (`t3/js2-lexer-module`, PR #752). `crates/js` is not changed. S2.5 needs two things from it: a tree of one function, and for each inner function the names that it uses from outside.

What it does:
- `parse_script` and `parse_module` give one tree of the whole text, as `crates/js` does. The tests use them.
- `parse_script_lazy` and `parse_module_lazy` give a tree of the top level only. Each function inside it is checked, not kept. The check finds every early error. It writes one `FnFacts` entry (`facts.rs`): the skip range, the captures (the outer names that it uses, one entry for each distinct name), `this`, `arguments`, `super`, `new.target`, direct `eval` and `with` flags, strictness, `length`, and the context at the start. The tree has `Body::Skipped(id)` for it.
- `parse_function(source, &mut facts, id)` gives the tree of one function from its facts. It finds each function inside it by its start offset (`Facts::find`, a binary search in the entries sorted by start) and the lexer jumps over its body. It adds no facts entry, and it does not pre-parse again. `Facts::preparsed` counts the bodies that were read in check mode; the tests and `parse_load fns` check that it does not change.

How the captures work. A name that an identifier expression uses goes on one stack (`refs`, 8 bytes each, only inside a function). A scope that closes removes the names that it declared (so a use before the `var`, `let` or function declaration is bound too). What a function leaves is its capture list, and it stays on the stack for the function around it. Entries are written when a function ends, so a function comes after the functions in it (`fns[sub..own]` are its descendants). The head of an arrow is read as an expression before `=>` shows that it is an arrow, so an arrow takes the stack and the entries from the start of its head (`(a, b = () => a) => ...`: the inner arrow belongs to the outer one and `a` is bound by its parameter). Rules: `arguments` is bound by a function that is not an arrow (it sets `ARGS` and is no capture); an arrow lists it. A function expression binds its own name; a class expression binds its name for its members. A class field initializer and a `static {}` block are functions for the names (their `this` is their own) and stay in the tree of the function around the class (`INLINE`, with their own entry). A direct `eval` (the name `eval`, not in parentheses, not `?.`) sets `EVAL` on the function and `INNER_EVAL` on every function around it. `with` sets `WITH`; a function in its body gets `IN_WITH`.

What a check-only body keeps. It builds nodes as the full parse does, and `parse_function_body` drops them after each statement (the arena goes back to the mark; the node count too). So the peak is the largest statement. A true no-node check is not built: the cover grammar (`(a, b) =>`, `[a] = x`) reads the nodes it has made. On real files the check costs 13% to 17% more instructions than the full parse (table below). The capture stack is most of it: the same build with the stack off gives 661 M on `index.js`, against 735 M with it and 644 M for the full parse (hypothesis for the cost: the name decode at each scope close and the sort of the lists at each function end; not profiled).

What changed in the copy of `parse.rs` and `ast.rs`:
- Gone: the regexp pattern check (`crates/js2` has no regexp engine; the lexer checks the flags; no case of the parse corpus has a bad pattern, and the test `regexp_pattern_gate` is not ported), `parse_data` and `ExprKind::Data` (the data literal of `crates/js`), the `Rc` source, the shared marks, `into_owned` and `Program::lazy_function`, `bare_observe`, the census hook, the `eager_at` and `in_class` rules (they kept arrows, async functions, generators, class members and functions after `(` or `!` out of lazy mode because the old evaluator needed their context; every function kind is skipped here), `LAZY_MIN_BODY` (a short body is skipped too; S2.5 can parse a short function at once, with `parse_function`).
- `max_nodes` counts the live tree: a dropped statement gives its count back. `crates/js` counted dropped bodies for the parse cache.
- A private name is not checked in `parse_function` (the class is not there; the first parse checked it).

Tests (`cargo test --locked -p bare-js2 --lib parse`: 67): 
- Ported from `parse_tests.rs`: 37 of the 38 tests (all except `regexp_pattern_gate`); `corpus_status_matches_acorn` runs the same 2,207-case corpus (1,233 accepted) unchanged. From `parse_lazy_tests.rs` I ported by idea, not by code: the body is skipped, an early error in a skipped body fails the parse (10 bodies compared with the full parse), the second parse gives the function of the first, strictness. Not ported: `these_functions_are_never_lazy` (the rule is gone) and `the_node_count_of_the_first_parse_still_counts_a_dropped_body` (replaced by `the_node_limit_counts_the_live_tree`).

| chain 10 | 244.22 M | 245.91 M | 246.11 M | 246.11 M | 12.58 MB | 12.58 MB | 12.58 MB |
| bodies 10 | 107.07 M | 108.28 M | 118.87 M | 223.66 M | 6.68 MB | 6.68 MB | 3.29 MB |

| Claude webview `index.js` (4.7 MB) | 692.3 M | 643.8 M | 735.2 M | 1,466.5 M | 38.9 MB | 38.9 MB | 7.4 MB |

| Postman `main.js` (1.9 MB) | 320.7 M | 260.1 M | 303.6 M | 627.3 M | 17.7 MB | 17.7 MB | 1.7 MB |

Reading the table:
- Peak memory: the pre-parse of a real file holds 5 to 10 times less than a full parse (38.9 to 7.4 MB, 17.8 to 1.8 MB, 17.7 to 1.7 MB). What stays is the top-level tree and the facts: `index.js` has 24,090 entries (23,220 pre-parsed bodies) and 43,101 capture names.
- Instructions: the new full parse is 0.3% to 19% below the old one on `stmts` and the three real files (7.0%, 11.6% and 18.9% on the real files), and 0.7% to 1.1% above on `chain` and `bodies`. Hypothesis, not checked: the regexp pattern check, the `bare_observe` span and the data-literal scan that `crates/js` runs and the copy does not. The pre-parse (`lazy`) costs 14%, 13% and 17% more than the new full parse on the three files, and about the same as the old full parse (+6%, -0.4%, -5%). So the pre-parse does not save instructions. It saves memory, and it gives the capture facts. Compiling every function once (`fns`) costs 2.2 times the full parse: the function bodies are read twice. A function that never runs is read once.
- `fns` makes 313,131 allocations on `index.js` (13 for each function parse: the arenas of a new `Parser` start empty). `lazy` makes 361. S2.5 can keep one parser's buffers (not done).

Not tested: the cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser); wall time; the Windows corpus tests; a second oracle for the captures (the tests state each expected list by hand; the sweep proves only that nothing fails and no function is read twice, not that the lists are right on real files); the Annex B rule (a function in a block is a `var` of the function; an extra capture can appear, a missing one cannot); direct `eval` that declares `var` in a sloppy function (flags only); the rows under glibc without `tcache_count`; macOS and arm64; the parser under Miri (it has no `unsafe`).

## 2026-11-20: bytecode format and verifier for `bare-js2` (plan step S2.4)

New modules in `crates/js2`: `bytecode.rs` (ops, encoder, decoder, the `Code` object, an assembler) and `verify.rs` (the verifier). No compiler and no interpreter yet (S2.5, S2.6). Base: main `bccb5b67`.

The format (details are in the module comment of `bytecode.rs`):

- One instruction is one 32-bit word `[op:8][a:8][b:8][c:8]`, plus one raw word `x` for 4 operands or for a compare-jump. A `Wide` prefix word makes the operands 16 bits (32 bits for a table index or an offset). `encode` picks the narrow form, so the compiler never names a width. 137 ops (the old format has 111).
- Constants are split by kind. Integers are immediates (`LoadI` 16 bits, `AddI` and the other `...I` ops 8 bits, the compare-jumps `J..I` 32 bits). `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` have no operand (`LoadNull`, `JSEqNull`, `JSNeUndef`, the 2-bit selector of `SetFieldK`, `JSEqB`). Atoms, other numbers, child functions and object-literal key lists have a table each.
- A property or global op names a site, not a name. `Code::sites[i]` is the atom of site `i`, and the per-realm feedback vector has one cache record at index `i`. A cache hit reads only the record, so `GetField dst, obj, site` is one word. The old op was two words (`AbcX`: cache number in `c`, name constant in `x`).
- Compare-jumps: `x === null` and its `undefined` forms are one word; a compare with an integer or an atom is two words (`x` is the operand); two registers are two words (`x` is the offset). Both polarities exist for `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, because `!(a < b)` is not `a >= b` for NaN. The equalities need one polarity.
- Loops: every jump back is `JmpBack`, every other jump goes forward. `JmpBack` is the budget check and a safepoint. `Code::loops` has one entry per header (the header and the last back edge), sorted. `Asm::finish` builds it from the `JmpBack` ops, so the JIT needs no loop discovery (design 6.11 item 19).
- Root maps: `Code::roots` is the `RootMaps` of S1.6. `Op::is_safepoint` says which ops need a map: every op except moves, loads, jumps and compares that cannot call JS, allocate or throw. `JmpBack` is one. The key is the `pc` of the first word. `roots.rs` gets two readers, `regs()` and `pcs()`, for the verifier.
- `Asm` (labels, `emit`, `jump`, `finish`) fills the jump offsets and chooses each width. A jump that does not fit 16 bits goes wide; widening one jump can push another over the limit, so the widths only grow until they stop changing.

The verifier checks: decoding and instruction starts; registers, windows (calls, literals, iterator records), special constants and each table index; unused fields are 0; each site has an atom and exactly one instruction; jump targets are instruction starts and only `JmpBack` goes back; the loop table; handlers; sorted source positions; a root map for each safepoint and for nothing else; and, by data flow over all paths, that no path runs past the end, the context depth agrees at joins, no instruction reads a register that a path has not written, and a root map names only registers that every path has written (this is what lets a frame skip the fill, design 6.10 item 4). It keeps one register set for each instruction, so it is for tests and debug builds.

Tests (22 new in `bytecode_tests.rs` and `verify_tests.rs`): an op-table consistency test; every op round-trips with narrow and wide values at the edges of each field (14 values, each field alone and all fields together), the narrow form is chosen when it fits, and an error writes nothing; sizes of the common instructions; decode errors; the assembler on forward and backward jumps, nested loops, two back edges to one header, and the cascade of widening (two jumps at the 16-bit edge); one test per class of verifier error, each with the exact message. Linux: `cargo test --locked -p bare-js2 --lib` 128 pass (106 on main). Windows 11 VM (`cargo xwin test`, exe through `winssh`): 128 pass. Both after the rebase on `bccb5b67`. `cargo clippy -p bare-js2 --all-targets`: no warning in the new files (`bare-os` and `heap.rs` have warnings that this change does not touch).

Code size against the old format. Method: the old compiler (`bc_gen_check`, in a scratch checkout of `e36a8dd4` with a dump added; not in the repository) compiled every function of jQuery 3.4.1 minified (a real minified library, 946 functions, 3 not compiled for direct `eval`) and of the 7 `eval_load` programs at scale 1 (59 functions). Each old instruction maps to one new instruction by the rules below, and the words are counted. This isolates the format. It does not include scope analysis, destination-driven registers, the effect context or switch tables (S2.5). Scripts and dumps: `/data/bare-tmp/s24/` (not in the repository).

- `GetField`, `SetField`: 2 words to 1 (2 when the function has more than 255 sites: 1 function of 946, 328 sites). `CallR`: 2 to 1. Compare-jump with `null` or `undefined`: 2 to 1; with an integer, an atom or a register: 2 to 2; with a non-integer number: 2 to 3 (`LoadN` first). `AddK` family: 1 to 1 for an 8-bit integer, 2 otherwise. `ClosureName`: 2 to 1. `GetEnv` and `SetEnv`: 1 to 1 (low) or 2 (high: every one is `GetCtxTdz`). `DefField` and `ArrayPush`: removed by `NewObjLit` and `NewArrLit` (low) or kept (high).

| Set | Functions | Old words | New words (low to high) | Change | Words per function, old to new |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| jQuery 3.4.1 minified | 946 | 47,934 | 35,664 to 42,593 | -25.6% to -11.1% | 50.7 to 37.7 / 45.0 |
| `eval_load`, 7 cases at scale 1 | 59 | 1,045 | 839 to 844 | -19.7% to -19.2% | 17.7 to 14.2 |

- In jQuery 47.2% of the old words are in 2-word instructions (`GetField` 25.2% of all words, `CallR` 14.2%). `GetEnv` is 9.6% and `Mov` 7.7%. The median function is 22.5 words, the 90th percentile 110, the maximum 2,907.
- The high bound counts every `GetEnv` as a dead-zone read. jQuery 3.4.1 is ES5 and has few `let` and `const`; a modern bundle has more, so its result is nearer the high bound (hypothesis).
- Two `eval_load` programs get larger by 1 word (`calls` 5 to 6, `loopfn` 11 to 12), and `closures` by 4 words at the high bound only. `fib` falls from 14 to 12 and `webpack` from 990 to 784. The constants of the larger ones (for example a modulus above 127) do not fit the 8-bit immediate, so `ModI` becomes `LoadN` and `Mod` (2 words, 2 dispatches). A wide `ModI` with a 16-bit immediate is also 2 words, and 1 dispatch. The interpreter (S2.6) can take that form.
- Tables and caches: the old `Code` holds a 24-byte `Const` for each constant and a 24-byte cache for each property op, in every code object. The new code has an 8-byte atom for each constant and a 4-byte site (hypothesis: one atom table entry for each old constant). Words, constants and caches together: jQuery 520,896 bytes to 226,920 to 254,636 bytes (-56.4% to -51.1%); `eval_load` (7 cases) 11,908 bytes to 5,364 to 5,384 bytes (-55.0% to -54.8%). The caches of the new engine are in the per-realm feedback vector, allocated on the second use, and are not counted: 8 to 16 bytes for each site that runs twice (design 6.10 item 12).
- Instructions: 36,391 old instructions in jQuery; `NewObjLit` and `NewArrLit` would remove 1,502 (4.1%). The other instructions map one to one, so the dispatch count of the format alone is 4.1% lower (low bound). The real change in dispatches depends on S2.5.
- Old `Wide` words: 282 of 36,391 instructions (0.77%) in this library, none of them `GetEnv`. The staging journey executed `Wide` for 1.6% of its ops (design 3.2); that journey is not available offline here.

Compared with QuickJS and Ignition (from `research-quickjs-reference.md` and `research-v8-reference.md`; the upstream sources were not read again):

| | QuickJS | V8 Ignition | `bare-js2` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | bytes, length set by the opcode | bytes | 32-bit words |
| Machine | stack (244 ops) | register with an accumulator | register, no accumulator (137 ops) |
| Larger operands | separate short and long opcodes; atoms are 32 bits in the stream | `Wide` and `ExtraWide` prefix bytes make all operands 2 or 4 bytes | one `Wide` prefix word; a table index or an offset has 32 bits |
| Constants | short forms of common pushes; atoms inline | `Smi` immediates, a constant pool, `LdaNull` and friends | immediates, per-kind tables, and a special-constant selector |
| Cache or feedback | none in the stream | slot operand, feedback vector for each closure | site operand; the feedback vector has the same index |

- Fixed words give up density in the narrow case: `Mov` is 4 bytes here and 3 in a byte format (hypothesis, not measured on the same code). They gain a decode that is one load and three shifts, no byte assembling, and jump offsets in words. The cost of a wide instruction is one extra word and one prefix dispatch. The old format already used this layout and measured 0.77% wide instructions on jQuery.

Judgment calls:

- The design (6.10 item 7) says atoms are inline in the word where they fit. An atom of `bare-js2` is the address of a cell (`atoms.rs`), 48 bits, so it cannot sit in a word. Atom operands are table indexes (8 or 16 bits), and a property name is the name of a site. A numeric atom id in S1.7 would allow inline atoms; I did not change S1.7.
- Both polarities of the relational compare-jumps and the integer-immediate forms make the op count grow from 111 to 137. Each extra op is one more interpreter arm. Hypothesis: the instruction-cache cost is small against the dispatches that they remove; S2.6 measures it.
- Only the iterator and loop ops that the core language needs are in the set. Classes, generators, destructuring, spread, regexp literals and templates add ops in S3 and S4. A new op needs one line in the table, and the verifier knows its operands from the letters.
- `Frames::walk` takes `&[RootMaps]`; the interpreter (S2.6) will hold the maps in `Code::roots`. I did not change `Frames`.

Not tested: a compiler or an interpreter on this format (S2.5, S2.6), so dispatch counts, instructions per op and the root maps of real functions are untested; the translation is static, by rules, and counts no dispatch weights; a modern React bundle (only jQuery 3.4.1 and the `eval_load` programs were available offline); Miri on the new modules (they hold no `unsafe`; the tests use `SharedAtoms`, which does); arm64; the cost matrix (js2 is not wired into the browser).
